speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL OF CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to announce the establishment of an advisory council of consumers which will advise me and my department on all matters of interest to the Canadian consumer. In doing so it will provide valuable assistance to the department in the administration of the Food and Drugs Act and the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act.
The council will consist of 15 members representing outstanding authorities and consultants in the consumer field across the country. The chairman will be Dr. C. A. Morrell, director of the food and drug directorate, and the secretary will be Miss Eleanor M. Ordway, chief of the directorate's consumer division.
The Food and Drugs Act is primarily a protective measure, in that its basic purpose is to protect the consuming public from injury or hazards to health, as well as from fraud in the manufacture, distribution and sale of food, drugs, cosmetics and therapeutic devices. The Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act is designed to protect the consumer from injury to health or from fraud with respect to registered proprietary medicines. In the administration of these two acts it has long been the practice, wherever possible, to seek the views of consumers on all matters of direct interest to them. With the development of more effective consumer organizations, 20220-379
whose views are becoming a strong influence as representative of consumer opinion, it was considered desirable to provide a more formal medium through which the department can be advised of consumer interests.
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to announce the names of those appointed to the council: Dr. M. Pernarowski, of Vancouver; Mrs. B. P. Marliss, of Edmonton; Dr. Edith Rowles, of Saskatoon; Mrs. W. Gilbert Weir, of Winnipeg; Dr. Barbara A. McLaren, of Toronto; Mrs. A.
F.	W. Plumptre, of Ottawa; Mrs. A. H. Zimmerman, of Ottawa; Madame J. F. Pilon, of Boucherville, Quebec; Mile. Huguette Pla-mondon, of Montreal; Madame Antonio Paradis, of Ancienne Lorette, Quebec; Madame Therese Casgrain, of Montreal; Mrs. H. R. Neilson, of Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Mrs. V. W.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL OF CONSUMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the appointment of this committee I think will commend itself generally; and as this is to be a committee that will look into consumer problems I hope it will be able to give some advice to the government regarding the ever rising costs of living, a matter of deep concern to all consumers across Canada. Any advice that the committee can give to the Minister of Finance and the department will certainly be welcome.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL OF CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this move to establish a consumers' advisory council is a step, albeit a very small step, in the right direction. The minister must be aware that the consumers association of Canada and the co-operative union of Canada have both asked for a government department to handle the increased activity in this direction. It is interesting to note that we have a government department to look after practically every economic group in the country such as agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining and so on. However consumers, who spend about $25 billion a year on personal goods in this country, do not receive the same sort of attention from the government that the other economic groups do.

Advisory Council of Consumers
I think in time, as a result ol pressure from the consumers' associations, the government will come to the point where a full scale department will be required to assist consumers in assessing the great variety of goods on the market at the present time. This is a step in the right direction, but it is a very faltering one, a very small step.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL OF CONSUMERS
speechtext:
We noted the remarks of the Minister of National Health and Welfare in announcing the establishment of this advisory council. She pointed out some of the functions of this council, and it seemed to me that most of the preliminary functions were the same as those of the food and drug administration which is now protecting the interests of the consumer. We feel that this council should have a somewhat wider scope, particularly in its set up so there would be representation of broader viewpoints on economic problems.
While we welcome the announcement that has been made concerning the functions that have been outlined by the minister, we do say it is only a very short step in the right direction, and that people who do take a broad interest in consumer problems should have a voice in this council.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make that I am sure will be of interest to all hon. members. During the past week a close watch has been kept on the sour cherry marketing situation, since it has been apparent that the crop will be particularly heavy both in Canada and the United States.
The crop in the United States is harvested somewhat earlier than that in Canada; unfortunately, however, the market in that country has been severely disrupted and late last week it became evident that unless appropriate action were taken much of the Canadian crop, which is grown almost entirely in Ontario, would remain unharvested because of the uncertainty of the future price situation. In this connection, it should be noted that the crop is used almost entirely for processing.
Immediate action has been taken to meet this situation, and I am pleased to be able to announce that governor in council authority is being sought to provide assistance under the Agricultural Stabilization Act to stabilize the price to producers of the 1964 crop of sour cherries delivered to processors at 7.8 cents per pound, which is 81 per cent of the ten year average or base price. Under the program for which authorization is sought, price stabilization will be accomplished by the agricultural stabilization board being authorized to make a direct payment to producers of 1.3 cents per pound of cherries.

Mr. Speaker, we are pleased to hear the announcement by the minister that price support will be provided for this particular commodity under the agricultural prices stabilization board, although we will have to assess, upon closer study, the value of the particular price that has been established. We are also pleased to see that members of the government, in spite of their opposition to this legislation and in spite of the comments they made during the election campaign, are now following the program we set out while we were in office. The Department of Transport is studying the question of ferry services between Nova Scotia and New England, and one factor it is reviewing is the volume of traffic carried on the M. V. Bluenose. TAX ON PRODUCTION MACHINERY IN OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: Does the government have any information with respect of a tax on production of machinery in the United States, England, Germany, France, Japan, and other countries in competition with Canadian industry?

subtopic: TAX ON PRODUCTION MACHINERY IN OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext: The United States, Britain and Japan do not have a sales or excise tax applicable to industrial production machinery. In France and Germany there is a turnover tax, which is the equivalent of a sales tax, levied on domestic and imported machinery. This tax amounts to 25 per cent in France and ranges from 4 per cent to 8 per cent in Germany. Other major industrialized countries whose manufactures compete with Canada's in world markets and who have taxes on industrial production machinery are Italy, Sweden and Switzerland. In Italy there is a turnover tax ranging from 4 per cent to 6J per cent. Sweden and Switzerland have general turnover taxes of 6.42 and 5.42 per cent respectively.

speechtext: In view of the fact that the American republics have signed a declaration condemning communist Cuba for aggression and approving the implementation of economic and diplomatic sanctions against her, has the Canadian government not received any direct word from the O.A.S. in relation to Canada's stand as it concerns this situation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: VANCOUVER, B.C.  CONTRACT FOR PAINTING VETERANS HOUSES
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CANADIAN ACTION TO RELIEVE TENSION
speechtext:
There has been no formal communication between the organization, or the meeting in Washington, and the government of Canada. I have an advance text of the principal resolution adopted yesterday at the ninth meeting of the consultative council of the foreign ministers of the O.A.S. countries. It was adopted by a vote of 15 to 4. In substance the resolution provides for the following measures against Cuba: that the governments of the American states shall not maintain diplomatic or consular relations with the government of Cuba; that they shall suspend all trade with Cuba except in foodstuffs, medicines and medical equipment; and that they

shall suspend all sea transportation with Cuba. There is a paragraph urging states not members of the O.A.S. that are animated by the same ideals of the inter-American system, to examine the possibility of effectively demonstrating their solidarity in achieving the purposes of the resolution.
Successive Canadian governments, in common with most other western governments, including virtually all members of NATO and the O.E.C.D., have consistently taken the position that diplomatic and trade relations do not signify approval of a particular regime. That continues to be the view of the government at the present time.
As we were not a participant in the discussions and decisions that have taken place in Washington we are not fully aware, of course, of all the considerations which may have been taken into account. We shall give careful study to the conclusions reached on the basis of such information as may be available to us. The house is aware that it has been the policy of this government, as it was of the previous government, to continue diplomatic and commercial relations with Cuba.
As far as trade is concerned, the export of arms and strategic materials to Cuba has been forbidden for several years; indeed, well before the decisions of this effect were reached by the O.A.S. itself in Washington on Saturday.

speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, the proportions requested in this resolution are intended to provide for all necessary requirements of the public service up to September 30. In no instance is the total amount of any item in the estimates released by the bill. I might add that the resolution and the bill are in the usual form, and I am prepared to give the usual undertaking that the passage of the resolution and the bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize or discuss any item in the estimates when it comes up for discussion in committee of supply, and the usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and not restricted or curtailed in any way as a result of the passage of this measure.
I would point out that the resolution provides for two months' interim supply covering all items in the main and supplementary estimates, except three items in the supplementary estimates. The reason those three items are excluded is that two of them in the supplementary estimates were passed and dealt with in a special appropriation bill some weeks ago, and the third item is one for which eleven twelfths had previously been granted by interim supply.
As to those items which have been set out in the resolution for which additional amounts over two twelfths are requested, on examination it will be seen that in general they are items where more work is being done in the summer as, for example, the east coast ferries,

Interim Supply
where the greater part of the expenditure is incurred in the summer season or, for example, in the case of a centennial project where the building is to be finished by September of this year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister one question at this stage. In the interim supply vote being asked for now is there an item reflecting the cost of Canada's military contribution to Cyprus?
I believe there is no such direct item. I would like to check that more fully, but I believe there is no direct item.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will that come forward subsequently as a further supplementary item, if it is not in this list?
I will check my answer more fully.

Mr. Chairman, the government is asking for interim supply for a period of two months, and I cannot remember when a government has gone for so long without passing its main estimates while continually having to ask for supply in order to carry on the business of the country.
You have a short memory.

Very few of the main estimates have been brought before this committee for consideration of the expenditures of the various departments. However, when interim supply is before the committee it gives members of parliament an opportunity to discuss many varied subjects.
One subject which has been neglected in discussion in this chamber is the problem of unemployment. We have waited patiently to see what the government intends to do about unemployment. Some 15 months have gone by since the government took office, and when we look at what it promised the Canadian people we find it has done literally nothing regarding unemployment. The government has bragged and proclaimed from time to time that unemployment has been dropping since it took office, but I would like to point out that unemployment has gradually decreased month by month since early 1961, when we were still in office. This is borne out by this year's budget white paper and by the Bank of Canada report, both of which showed that unemployment has decreased month by month since early 1961, and this is directly as a result of the policies of the former government. This government has ridden on that wave of improvement and has endeavoured to take the credit, but it has done nothing to try to improve the position substantially.
[Mr. Mcllraith.l
During the last election members of the government said unemployment was one of the most urgent economic problems facing the country and promised they would do something about it. When we were in office the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the statesman for Essex East, continually berated us for not dealing, in his words, substantially with the problem. There were others who took up those cudgels day after day, and I remember on one occasion they spent as long as eight days on one item to provide finances for the municipal winter works program, which at that time they despised and criticized so much. Now they have adopted that program and feel it is going to cure unemployment. In this connection I would point out that the municipal winter works program has increased in scope annually since its inception in the winter of 1958-59.
If we look at the latest unemployment figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics we find that in June 1962 there were
308,000	Canadians unemployed; in June 1963 there were 304,000, and in June this year, despite the fact that the government claims unemployment is not any longer a national problem, there were 282,000 Canadian unemployed.
In the opinion of this government unemployment has been cured in this country simply because there are 22,000 Canadians fewer unemployed today than there were last year, and 26,000 fewer than in 1962. What does it mean in terms of percentages? This year unemployment is .4 per cent less than last year, and less than one half of 1 per cent lower than in 1962; it is .5 or one half of 1 per cent lower than in 1963. This, the present government says, amounts to a cure of unemployment. Unemployment, they claim, has been licked; it is only a regional problem.
Well, if you want to look at it in that way and not from a national viewpoint, this has been the case for many years past. But when members opposite say this is a regional problem and that they have cured unemployment in this country, I invite them to look at the situation in the province of Quebec. According to figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics for the month of June, unemployment in the province of Quebec in 1963 resulted in 113,000 people being out of work. This year the figure is 105,000, or 8,000 less than a year ago. This, members opposite claim, amounts to the cure of unemployment. Unemployment, as far as they are concerned, has been licked. As a

matter of fact they have dropped the problem of unemployment in the same way they would drop a hot potato.
Let us take a closer look in the way in which they have dealt with the unemployment situation. Let us examine the figures issued by the d.b.s. for June, 1964 as they concern young people under 19 years of age. First of all, in June, 1963, there were 94,000 unemployed in that category. In June of this year the figure was 103,000. In other words there were 9,000 more young people of this country unemployed than there were a year ago.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, has this government cured unemployment? We do not know what is in the offing in the days to come. Certainly the 22,000 difference in total on the Canadian scene as between this year and last year is nothing to brag about. I must say that on the face of these figures the present government has failed miserably to deal with the unemployment problem in this country, and has not put forward any program for doing so. In fact members opposite have no policy of any kind for dealing with unemployment, and I have yet to hear their spokesmen come forward with a long range plan to deal with it.
They did, of course, establish the depressed areas. They themselves singled out these depressed areas, and in order to create new employment there they set up a Department of Industry. We quizzed the Minister of Industry about the results. We asked him how many new industries had been established in these designated depressed areas, but the hon. gentleman was very evasive. He talked about industries which contemplated settling in those areas, but said nothing definite. When pressed, he had nothing to say.
Mr. Chairman, we can only come to one conclusion, and it is this. The biggest industry which has been created in Canada under this proposal has been the Department of Industry itself, because we learn from the figures available to us that more than 500 people are employed in that department. This is the extent of the government's achievement in setting up industry in Canada. Instead of setting up industry in depressed areas where there is need for employment of Canadians, they have set it up in Ottawa. Consequently I have come to the conclusion, and I think there are many who agree with me, that the depressed area must be Ottawa because of this government which is in office.
Hon. members opposite tried to camouflage the issue back in June, 1963, when the Min-
Interim Supply
ister of Labour outlined what he termed nine definite plans to combat unemployment. When we look closer at all these plans which were announced by him at that time we find they were all, in the main, proposals which had been initiated by the former government. In order to train the unemployed we established the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act under which we helped to build up the necessary facilities. What was done during the period of time we were in office? In 1962-63 there was a total expenditure of $179,626,976 on these projects. In the fiscal year 1963-64 there was an expenditure of $102,037,672. The total expenditure since the inception of this program in December, 1962 amounted to $352,533,151.
Then this government came to office and amended the act in November, 1963. This was supposed to give the program a new impetus. What has been the result? From November 30 of that year to June 30, 1964, the total expenditure incurred by the federal government amounted to $14,869,410. That is all that has been done by this government in connection with this program. I think this government should look carefully at the possibilities of this program. I think it is about time they launched upon the building of technical schools for the purpose of training adults, particularly those who find themselves out of employment because of automation and technological change.
The second scheme was one for the training of unemployed workers. This was a program started from scratch when we took office, and in 1962 a new impetus was given to it; a new opportunity was afforded to Canadians to train themselves and acquire new skills. What has been done by the present government since it took office? In answer to a question I put on the order paper some interesting figures were supplied. I asked how many people had completed their training during 1963 under the plan for the training of unemployed workers. In reply we were told that 32,825 people were enrolled under this program during 1963, that 17,627 completed their training during that year and 9,928 were still in training at the end of that year. My second question asked how many had completed their training under this plan during the year 1962, and the answer was that 27,895 were enrolled under the program in the year 1962; 13,753 had completed their training during that year, and 7,778 persons were still in training at the end of the year.
What is the total advance made in connection with this program? What has justified

Interim Supply
the boasts of hon. members opposite that they would give it new life? A total of some 5,000 persons were enrolled in all of Canada beyond the number enrolled in 1962, and some 4,000 more completed their training in that year. This is all they were able to accomplish during that period of time after inheriting a program which we had initiated and established.
The third point the minister mentioned concerned the re-employment of older workers. We know how that program fared. The response was negligible. About 1,000 people got jobs under this program in all Canada. I am sure the minister should look very closely at this particular program with a view to lifting many of the restrictions which are now in force so as to give an opportunity for more of these older workers to find employment. I think a program designed to educate employers would probably be far more effective than any bonuses which might be offered to encourage employers to hire older workers.
Then there was the program of capital assistance to provide technical training facilities. This is a program which has not gone anywhere yet; there has been no impetus to it. I remember that at the time the act was amended this measure was supposed to give an opportunity to the province of Quebec to catch up to Ontario in its building program, but such has not been the case since November 30 of last year.
Then there is the item with regard to technological change and manpower development. We have not heard anything in regard to this program. There has been no conference called of industry and labour to see whether this type of program could get moving. All the government is doing is working from the old provincial agreements and the clauses contained therein. This program needs an impetus, a push in order to help people who are affected by automation and technological change. This government has not lifted a finger to do anything about it. All they did was make an announcement and let it go at that.
That is the way this government have been operating since they took office. We have only had legislation put through in a hurry in order to show the Canadian people they are doing something, and in those instances they have had to withdraw, completely cancel or modify the legislation to the extent that you could not even recognize it as the legislation that was originally introduced.
Then there is the promotion of winter house building, the $500 building bonus for winter

built houses. This, I must acknowledge, has had some effect, because if I remember correctly 28,000 homes were built under this program. But it has now had a detrimental effect on the house building industry, because many of those people who were engaged in the building of homes during the winter months have been laid off; and in view of the fact that the announcement has already been made that this program will be continued in the ensuing winter months, many people are hesitant about building their homes in the summer as they normally would. Consequently we now have a sag in the house construction industry of this country.
We do not hear any more about the $7 million that the federal government announced as item No. 7 in their program to create employment opportunities. Nothing further has been heard of that program. How many of these projects have been undertaken to help the unemployed of this country? Then there is the extension of the municipal winter works program. I mentioned this earlier. This was item No. 8. This program has been gradually increasing in impetus and more municipalities have been participating in the program year after year, winter after winter. It is a good program and will continue to expand as the years go by; therefore it should be kept on the books.
No. 9 was the strengthening of personnel resources as this affects the placement officers in the national employment service. We do not know how many of these new personnel have been recruited and are now actively engaged in placing people in employment. Not too long ago the Minister of Labour announced that the national employment service was going to come under the wing of the Department of Labour, but that is all that has happened and we have heard nothing since. There has been no word, no report as to what has happened, and as far as I know the national employment service is still under the unemployment insurance commission. I think the minister should tell us what is happening in this field and what has been done to carry out the recommendations contained in the Gill commission report.
And what about the Gill commission report? Why has nothing been done about that? Why have not amendments been brought forward to implement the Gill commission report? What is going to happen this coming winter? How is the fund going to stand up? Is it going to go broke again? Will they keep on hiding the fact that it is going to go broke,

as they did this past winter; or will they come back to parliament and ask for more money? Why the hesitation? Why have they not taken action to strengthen the Unemployment Insurance Act on the basis of the recommendations made by the Gill commission, so this fund could go back to the basis upon which it operated originally?
Then at the end of last year we had the report of the Norris commission. On the basis of that report the government set up trustees over shipping operations on the great lakes. But since the trustees were appointed, Mr. Chairman, the Norris commission report has been completely ignored and thrown out the window. Nothing further has been done with regard to the recommendations made by Mr. Justice Norris. We in the House of Commons begin to wonder about the position in this regard. We are told that parliament set up the trustees and they are responsible to parliament and parliament only. The minister abdicates every responsibility in respect of this matter. When you ask him questions as to the activities of the trustees and what has been done in this regard, he completely evades his responsibility. He suggests it is none of his responsibility and says he will convey our views to the trustees. In what capacity is he acting in this regard?
A good messenger boy.

What is the Minister of Labour doing? Is he acting as a minister of the crown responsible for this piece of legislation that he piloted through the House of Commons, or is he acting only as a messenger boy and abdicating all his responsibility? That is the only conclusion we can come to after listening to the answers the minister has given.
We want to know what deal was made with Paul Hall, the president of the seafarers' international union in the United States; because some sort of satisfaction was given to him in view of the fact that he has not uttered a sound of late, after previously making all the threats possible. It is fine to have peace on the great lakes, but at what price, Mr. Chairman? This is what we want to find out when we ask the minister to bring the trustees before the standing committee on industrial relations.
In this respect, Mr. Chairman, why does not the minister add his own request to that of the members of parliament; or is he going to allow the trustees, by refusing to appear before this committee, by refusing to appear before the members of this parliament to
Interim Supply
answer some of the questions that are in the minds of members of this house, to defy the parliament that appointed them and set up this system? Even though the minister wants to have only the role of a messenger boy in this respect, I think he has an obligation as a member of the government, as the Minister of Labour, to bring to the attention of the trustees the fact that this matter is vitally important; that members should have the opportunity of questioning the trustees on their activities in respect of this very important and vital matter.
We read a great deal about what is happening, and we have to get information second hand. There is no reason at all why members of parliament should not have the trustees appear before them in the industrial relations committee. If the trustees feel that any information they wish to give to members of that committee would be detrimental to the work they are undertaking at the moment, and would be detrimental to peace on the great lakes, I am sure the members would agree that this meeting should be held in camera. After all, the members of this house have a responsibility in this regard. They were concerned with the setting up of the trusteeship and should now have the opportunity, because of their responsibility in this matter, of questioning these people to see what kind of a job they have done for us. I think the less delay there is in this connection, the better it will be.

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member for Port Arthur speaks, I wonder whether I might have a moment to correct what may have been a wrong impression I gave the committee a few moments ago.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had asked me whether there was any item in these estimates which dealt with the Cyprus operation. Mr. Chairman, this bill gives us what may be the last reasonable opportunity to raise grievances, and I would assume that some of my colleagues will raise grievances although we also hope that it will be possible to get this measure through in a couple of days so we can get on with

what promises to be the high point of the session, the flag debate.
Anyone watching the political scene must be having a bit of a wry chuckle over the flag. Our economy has not been in such a good position for quite a number of years. It seems to me that you would have to go back to 1955 to find an economic situation as good and equable as at the present time. It is usually considered unfair or almost indecent for a member of the opposition to make such a comment, but this summer my mail of discontent which most often reflects our economic imbalance is very small. This and other contacts I have had with my riding have led me to believe that our economy at the present time, whatever the minor difficulties-and I think there are some in some areas-is in rather good shape compared with what it has been in over the last few years.
It seems to me that the wryness and irony come from the fact that despite this situation I cannot find any tremendous satisfaction with the present government. This seems to me to indicate something which I think was also noted in 1956 and 1957 as the Liberal government of that day moved toward its downfall; that it is not the economic factors which finally lead to the determination of how people will vote or will shift their vote; it is other things. In that case it was the whole issue of the rights of parliament and a developing arrogance within the administration. This summer it seems to me that the discontent focusses on the performance of this parliament and on some of the questions which have been left unanswered by the government and which have very little to do with economics or with the topic of which the hon. member who preceded me spoke.
I am referring to the situation which the government seems to have reached whereby it has given the impression that it is giving away its powers and initiative; whereby this place, the commons and parliament, the real centrepiece of the country, is being replaced by the federal-provincial conference. It seems to me this is one of the reasons for the discouragement and the malaise which exist at the present time; the feeling that there is not a strong hand at the centre, that there is not a willingness to give the kind of strong national leadership which the country wants. There seems instead to be a predisposition to dispose of power through all kinds of negotiation.
What better reflection can you get of this than the display last week in the debate on

student loans. That was a measure which in the main was quite unsatisfactory in its limitations to those of us who supported it; it was also opposed by another group in the house who, perfectly within their rights, took a completely different interpretation of it because of the particular views which reigned in one province. So we are left with each side dissatisfied on this issue. Those of us who wanted a better bill with lower interest rates, with scholarships and bursaries of a genuine kind, had to settle for something quite inadequate, and our friends from Quebec had to settle for a formula which still leaves them in doubt about this so-called cooperative federalism.
It is that kind of division which indicates the inability of this government to come up with strong leadership. I noticed one of our commentators thought it was a reflection on the performance of this house that during the debate on student loans none of the English speaking members made any kind of suggestion as to how in this particular bill we could better satisfy our French Canadian friends. I think one of the reasons all of us hesitate to enter that field is because it is so controversial.
I might point out that in this particular field our government has not given us leadership. I cannot think of any better example of the gap there is in federal leadership than the fact that the majority of the English speaking people in this country want stronger leaders and leadership in the field of education, particularly higher education and education to meet the advance in technological change and automation. The people are not getting this leadership. Instead, on almost every front, but particularly the education front, we seem to have to settle for the kind of displacement of these issues and problems from parliament out into the federal-provincial conference. This is so not only in the educational field but in other fields as well.
Therefore if effective negotiations in this country are going to take place in federal-provincial conferences, and if effective studies and investigations and reports in this country are going to be made by royal commissions or specially selected academicians, this means that we are nothing more than a buzz chamber to make annoying noises, or noises of annoyance, the majority of the time. Many of us feel that this government is distributing or negotiating away the leadership and power which many of us thought were centred here.

I cannot give a better illustration of the inadequacy of the government in the leadership field than the matter of redistribution, which many people think is a minor thing or, if not a minor thing, a matter of such partisan character that it is just as well to leave it alone and not get too excited about it. Yet the fact remains that we have every chance of another election on the unfair basis of the 1951 census. It seems to me that the point of democracy is to give simple justice to the simple voter. You start with the principle of one man and one vote and some kind of balance between the value of votes cast anywhere in the country. This is of paramount importance. Yet we have had nothing from the government but lip service to this idea. We have had no real action or persistence.
No guts.

As my hon. friend says, no guts on something which really gets to the roots of where one stands as an individual in a democracy. We have all kinds of guts on the flag issue but no guts on redistribution. It seems to me that while the one may be of symbolic importance, the other is a continuing thing inherent in the rights of each of us as a citizen of this country. Yet redistribution goes by the way.
One of the arguments put forward by my friend from Ontario who spoke before me related to the S.I.U. I cannot think of any better illustration than the S.I.U. situation of the way we have been bamboozled over the rights which we have as members of parliament. All of us got worked up into almost a paroxysm of righteousness last summer about straightening out Hal Banks and the S.I.U. By jove, we were going to bring good old Canadian decency into labour relations on the great lakes. I think all of us got worked up in a sort of phony exultation that we would put this kind of United States racketeer in his place. We had many deliberations about the kind of trustees we would have, and so on. I feel a little stupid about this, but I actually recommended privately to the Minister of Labour that he choose Charles Millard as one of the trustees. I have been feeling very badly about how wrong I was in that recommendation. Aside from this, we created the trustees but we were not vigilant enough to realize that we had no means of seeing, of following and watching, the kind of job they were going to do.
Obviously we now have a situation where one of the trustees is really in effect in charge,

where the head of the board of trustees really would like to give up the job and get back to beautiful, bounteous British Columbia-* his health is not too good-and where one of the other trustees has a number of other jobs in labour relations and really has been giving very little time to these duties. We have a situation where almost every member of the house has had some case brought to his attention in connection with the S.I.U. indicating that the reforms we expected and wanted just have not come about. Instead we have the statement by one trustee that Leonard McLaughlin has been morally regenerated, and all the minister seems to be able to do in this whole situation is indicate that there is the act, the trustees report to parliament, they do not have to come before parliament, and really he would not want to press them too hard.
I do not think anything the hon. member for Ontario has said in this regard is too strong. In effect, perhaps through our own stupidity we have been bilked on this whole S.I.U. situation. I believe firmly that some kind of deal has been made informally by the minister or his representatives with Paul Hall and the United States union. The price has been what all of us want, peace on the great lakes for this summer; but from the evidence that is coming in it would appear that individuals who have been persecuted in the past are now trapped in the middle of the S.I.U. web, and I am afraid that basically the plan has not changed. As the price for peace what we are getting is a continuation of the kind of attitude that Hal Banks represented, even though Hal Banks has been shifted off to one side.
I suggest this is another example of why so many of us do not see the kind of strong, vigorous leadership with which everyone was crediting the government when they brought in the legislation last summer. I think we have to accept some of the responsibility in this regard because we were certainly remiss in letting this trusteeship be established without the kind of review that it is now apparent is necessary. When the government selects trustees and places them on a board and they do not measure up and are not good enough, it is obvious that this assembly through one of its committees needs some kind of investigating or review power to see if we cannot get some changes.
Of all the leadership aspects so far as the present government is concerned the most disappointing really has to do with what the Prime Minister had to say, I suppose facetiously, about the new politics. We were going

to have the new politics in this chamber. The whole thing was prefaced by the wonderful new arrangement that was going to bring democracy into the Liberal party caucus through the striking of advisory committees to the various ministers. Advise him?
And advise him. I cannot say this has broken down, but I would be willing to bet a thousand dollars it has broken down and disappeared and is not in effect.

I do not think it really ever started. But this was part of the new politics. We were going to get this new politics and part of it was to be a falling away of partisanship. We were going to get a new spirit within the House of Commons and in the whole party picture, led, one supposed, by a noble, high minded and idealistic Prime Minister. We have got the new politics all right, and it seems to be pretty well the same old game.
The whole question of leadership in parliamentary reform seems to have gone by the board. On the one hand we have the Prime Minister insisting that if there is anything wrong with the operation of the House of Commons it is not because of a lack of good intentions on his part or on the part of his followers. It is the wicked opposition, particularly that wicked fellow, that dreadful character who leads the official opposition. The fact remains, Mr. Chairman, that you cannot bring about any reform or radical changes in this place unless the Prime Minister is willing to put his reputation and that of his party and the government on the line to get these reforms. So we have had nothing but sweet talk at the start of the session about the new politics, and no substantial leadership in this connection.
The whole question of parliamentary reform splits people in this chamber within the various parties, and most often on the basis of how long they have been here. It seems that the longer a member has been here the more he is opposed to any drastic parliamentary reform. I notice that the newer members are very much in favour of reform. I see the Secretary of State for External Affairs shaking his head. I should like to tell him that one gets reports-you know

the kind of reports that filter around this place-about the real stumbling blocks to any parliamentary reform. Do you know persons on the government side who we hear are the real stumbling blocks? The Minister of Transport and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I just thought I would mention that.

I know you are Liberal minded, with a capital "L". The "L" is so big that you cannot climb over it and down the other side.

speechtext: I hope the hon. member's reports are more authentic than the minister's.

I think they are. A great many of the newer and younger members feel very strongly that there should be some changes in the procedures of the house and in its whole make-up. I want to offer a suggestion. We are going to have to think about more than just minor procedural changes. It seems to me that if we are ever going to get the reforms that so many members appear to be seeking, reforms which will give members the opportunity to do a bigger job than they have done up to the present, we are going to have to consider such things as moving toward a separation of the executive from the legislative assembly. We are going to have to consider giving our parliamentary committees the kind of power we have never considered before.
Would the hon. gentleman clear that up? How under our parliamentary system are you going to separate the executive and the legislative? I am interested in that.

Very easily; by changing the system and separating them. That is what I am suggesting. I remember that in 1958 when the right hon. gentleman was prime minister he announced that he was going to bring about some reforms in the committees. He was frank enough to acknowledge that he had never been an enthusiast for committees, but he said he intended to see if something could not be done with them.
I suggest that the experience of that parliament and the subsequent ones in really turning house committees into active forums with real influence on policy and with real investigatory powers has not been successful. I am not blaming him; I am blaming the

system. I do not see how you can give parliamentary committees greater powers than they have at the present time without upsetting the balance and the control of the party by the leadership of the cabinet within the house. But I should like to suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that during the years he has sat in this place he has seen parliament become much less the circumference of government and much more just a little piece of the pie, a slice of a big pie which is big government, a government in which the Prime Minister and the cabinet tend to be the dominating factors on the political level and the administrators on what I consider to be perhaps the most important level, the work of carrying out decisions.
It seems to me that the British parliamentary system has a very grave and basic weakness as our government tends to more and more complexity.

May I ask this question? I am very interested in following what the hon. gentleman has said. Certainly in the United Kingdom and elsewhere where the parliamentary system is in effect the trend has been toward a stronger and stronger executive dominating parliament. A few moments ago the hon. member was asking for strong government, but I come back to his very interesting suggestion that we should adopt a system whereby the executive would be freed from the legislative and administrative responsibility that now rests with it.
I should like to know what he has in mind. I am not asking for the purpose of embarrassing the hon. member. I know he has given very careful study to this subject, and I would be interested in what he has in mind as to how to remove the executive from the legislative responsibility of parliament.
The right hon. gentleman raised first a minor point that is quite important-
This is an extraordinary suggestion.

It may be an extraordinary suggestion. However, early in his remarks the right hon. gentleman raised one point that I should clear up. He said I was complaining about the lack of strong leadership from this government. I want to make the point that this government has not, in my mind, given strong leadership but it has all the facilities for giving strong leadership. It is so buttressed and protected by the inherent power it has through cabinet powers that we really cannot get working at it critically.

I suggest to the right hon. gentleman we are faced with this situation. If we cannot get committees of this house with the power and with the assiduity to really be able to investigate the administration, and if we cannot really do something about the legislation that is brought before us in terms of getting changes and amendments, then I suggest we really haven't got much to do in committees. If we do give committees the power and do not change our system to a point where they are separate from the executive, then we destroy the whole principle of ministerial responsibility and party responsibility as it is known within the British system.
I am not suggesting that we should immediately consider the United States congressional system, but I suggest that is probably the only way out if we want to give to members of parliament a bigger role. Perhaps we should not have a bigger role. Perhaps we should continue to be sort of swallowed up by trivia and then, like an appendix, eventually somebody will take us out and throw us away. I think in many ways that is tending to be the choice that faces us.
I suggest, for example, that the public accounts committee as it is now constituted is doing the best job of any of our committees. If we gave that committee real power in terms of recommendations, and real power in being able to direct government policy in these particular areas, we would immediately have to amend the whole cabinet system. Where would a minister stand; where would a senior official stand if a parliamentary committee had that power? One of the things that has bothered me about recommendations for reform is that they generally come down to two things; let us limit debate, and let us give the committees more to do.
Well, let us start with the second point. If you give the committees more to do, it seems to me you can only do so at the peril of the cabinet system of ministerial responsibility, unless you turn out a new type of platonic politician who will not take party advantage within a parliamentary committee. I do not suggest this is possible.
Let us consider the other part, the relationship of the executive toward parliament, to see if it may not be possible to separate them or at least to see where we are going. I do feel that there is a more efficient quality in the United States congressional system than a lot of the snobs amongst our political scientists would credit. I think their system works in a democratic way much better than many of us think. I believe some of the

limitations of the United States system are not as real as some of us have felt, particularly during the McCarthy crisis when the senator was running wild with a senate committee.
I wanted to touch again on this question of limitation of debate. The last time I mentioned the question in the house, because I suggested the government had a responsibility in connection with the possibility of resorting to closure, the members of the official opposition were delighted and some of my friends were irritated and distraught, to put it mildly. I want to return to this particular point, not to make it again but I hope to make it more clearly. In essence, the way our system is set up the government has the initiative in determining the parliamentary business. I think the opposition is quite limited here. The right hon. gentleman who led the previous government made no changes in the system when he met the whole problem of the introduction of closure. I for one think there should be a better way of arriving at some limitation of debate than closure. I suggest that this is another field where negotiations have really not been entered into with any great fairness.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask him what he considers would be the gain for parliament if any kind of limitation of debate were adopted. What is the objective?

I suppose the simplest objective would be to ease some of the criticism that exists about the length of time we spend talking. However, I do not think that is the kernel of the problem. It seems to me we have a situation where an immense amount of legislative work has to be put through. The sheer quantity of the pile-up lengthens the session so that some kind of prearrangement is needed. We get bogged down because each one of us, in our party terms, is trying to take the most advantage of a loose and fluid situation. This is one of the reasons, it seems to me, why the prearrangement for limitation of debate on legislative items would be worth while.
The other area in which we can lengthen debate interminably is an area such as this

or on the supplementary estimates, which is comparable; in other words when we are looking at the spending program of the government. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre knows that when we are contemplating estimates most of us do not spend our time telling the government how to cut down its expenditures. We spend our time telling them how they can spend more money.
That is a socialist.

I know a fellow from Bow River who gets very socialistic when it comes to spending in his riding. I recall that there was a penitentiary to be built somewhere out there, and I recall the member for Bow River insisting that the penitentiary should not be built anywhere else. He was not insisting, for instance, that the penitentiary should be built in the maritimes, where they need it more.
You have not been out to Drumheller; you do not know anything about it.

It all depends on where you stand on these things. Let me get back to this question of the estimates. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and other veterans in the house have suggested at times that this kind of work should go to the estimates committees. The trouble with committees is that they do not develop in this way. I was on an estimates committee a few years ago which was very ably chaired by the hon. member for Calgary North. The disturbing thing was that we would spend 20 days on a department, but after reporting back in the house it did not seem to make any difference at all to the length of the debate. At that time hon. members on that side were sitting on this side, and the fact that the department had been considered by the estimates committee did not seem to make any difference.
I think you would agree that you fellows took up a great deal of time in debate.

The hon. gentleman has said that my friends took up a lot of time. Yes, we took up a lot of time. Everybody takes up a lot of time, it seems to me. This is the subject to which I am referring. How can you shift some of this speaking time out of here? I suggest again that if you are going to have the estimates reviewed by a committee, the committee has to be supported

by some kind of power so it is really not necessary to come back here and review the estimates again.
Here again I do not see how you can give a committee this kind of power without putting in jeopardy our cabinet system and whole tradition of party responsibility. It is for that reason I think it is time the Prime Minister, who has been willing to talk about the new politics and pinpoint the Leader of the Opposition as being so destructive to this place and its practices, came forward with something more than the phrases "new politics" and "co-operative federalism" and told us what he would do to change and improve this place.
Nothing.

Someone interjects "nothing", and I am afraid that is what we are going to get. That is the substance of my remarks, that this is likely what we will get from the government. As I pointed out early in my remarks, the government seems to have lost its purpose at the very time the economy seems to be doing most well.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to speak at length, but I heard, during the discussion of interim supplies, some talk of unemployment in Canada and that there had been no substantial improvement in this field.
I do not want to speak of unemployment in a critical way, but I want to make some suggestions to the government which, I think, might improve the situation in fields where perhaps no suggestion was ever made. They are based on the fact that Canadian workers are leaving the factories in ever greater numbers to be replaced by machines. They must find work somewhere.
I have established a rather limited list-to which, of course, additions might be made- of those fields where more Canadian citizens might gradually find employment.
I shall, for instance, start with the Department of Public Works. There is a new development in this field, and it is with new ideas that we shall find a solution to our problem. Lately, I received a report on the trans-Canada highway, which extends over
4,000	miles and is partly finished. In this respect, I shall make a suggestion which will give employment to a great number of Canadian citizens, because, there again, the government is in charge of that highway. Why should we not enact legislation to landscape this highway, for instance by planting trees
Interim Supply
and flowers and establishing camping grounds along the road?
This is something which does not yet exist but which could be tried in order to create new jobs for the Canadian citizens who are today unemployed.
This is but one example, but precisely because I have several examples of this kind of offer, I am requesting the government to try to develop those fields that are not developed today.
Let us take another example; this one concerns the Secretary of State and is about the national film board. In this connection, the Secretary of State could see to it that we have Canadian full-length or feature films, which are practically non-existent today. Next week we shall have the national film festival, and most of the films shown will come from foreign countries. We, Canadians, shall not even have a full-length film to show during this national film festival.
How does it happen that Canada, which has embarked on modern developments, will show, in this film festival, only Italian, American, German, Japanese, English and Russian films, but no Canadian film? Why? Because Canada has no full-length film industry. We have the national film board, which has certainly progressed considerably but, unfortunately, is far from being up to date in this field.
In the framework of the national film board, or of another similar agency, we should have a much more intense and rational development of the film industry, and this to achieve a full-length film industry. That would offer several advantages and contribute to the development of our technicians, of whom we do not have enough yet. That would promote the training of artists, tragedians, actors, directors, cameramen, etc. and lead to opportunities for a great number of Canadian citizens.
Another field which is perhaps better developed today than it used to be, but to which great improvements could be made, and which would create many jobs, would be, and this concerns the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), that of medical research. Of course, there is medical research in Canada today, but compared to the research carried on in other countries such as France, England, Germany, Italy, we are lagging.
We do not have enough doctors, scientists, chemists, physicists working in laboratories, specially in medical research. That is an-

Interim Supply
other field which the Minister of National Health and Welfare could develop.
The Secretary of State, for its part, is responsible for the Canada Council. The Canada Council has surely done a lot but it must be recognized that it had the advantage of a budget, seven or eight years ago, but since then, there has not been much change. Nothing was done to allow the Canada Council to help more. There again, the Canada Council does not develop in proportion with the development of the country. Yet, many jobs could be developed there which would serve Canadian citizens, in the field of symphonic orchestras and opera for instance. We do not have yet in Canada a single professional opera company which would play all year round, when other countries have theirs. We do not have one yet which gives performances of a professional quality, on a permanent basis. We have only opera companies which play now and then when it is admitted that opera must be part of a developed civilization and culture, and we really deplore this situation. Canada has not even made a start-let us say it has barely started-in that field.
I admit that the Canada Council is of some assistance there, but I feel that the government should give much larger subsidies to the Canada Council, so that it may help the development of theatre groups, symphony orchestras, etc. Many developments might be achieved in the field of arts at a time when we find that our professional artists need help. Canada might be a nursery of artists if more subsidies were granted in that field.
Another field-and I think it is under the responsibility of the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson)-concerns the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which grants subsidies and helps the construction of homes.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should also play a role, in addition to that one, and attempt to develop architecture more completely. To build houses is not everything. Indeed, similar houses, one after the other, can become monotonous in our communities.
Why does not the corporation have available town planners and specialized architects who, besides looking after the building of houses, would be interested in housing developments where life would be pleasant, and where some green and trees would be planned? Why not see about developing a Canadian architecture, and not an architecture like the one we see nowadays financed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, where all houses are alike?

Why not start new developments where architects and town planners could go to it merrily and try out new models of houses, and carry out a complete redevelopment? Those are improvements and innovations to which the federal government could also contribute.
Mr. Chairman, I know that in all the fields I mentioned since I started my remarks, not one concerns directly and immediately the necessities of life, or even the useful things of life, but in a parliament such as ours, unfortunately, we do not think enough about the things that could make life more agreeable, such as town planning and architecture.
For instance, in the field of health, the former government had created a special fund for amateur sport. It was a small beginning. The door was half-opened but unfortunately, that does not go far enough. Naturally, the committee looking after amateur sport, which in English is called the Canada physical fitness council, does not have the funds required to do an important job. Indeed, the development in this field of endeavour, in this country, is only starting and there is a shortage of qualified instructors in practically every municipality. Only a few localities and institutions managed to get some, but the amount of money made available to the physical fitness council to subsidize interprovincial and international games, as well as the building of playgrounds, gymnasiums and swimming pools, is too limited to allow for the hiring of qualified supervisors and instructors.
At the present time, the Canada physical fitness council is getting very little money. Why? Because budgets are too limited in that field.
The same situation applies as far as the Canada Council is concerned, because subsidies in the field of art are too limited. There should be a lot more grants so that not only the useful side, the strict necessities of life could be considered, but also the things which make life more pleasant for people in general.
Mr. Chairman, there is also the development of national parks. Our national parks are developing slowly, but we just have to go to other countries to see how parks and camping grounds are being created at a much quicker pace than in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, if the required improvements were made in every field I just mentioned, we would not only create many jobs, but also open the people's eyes on a new culture, a more developed civilization, in

brief, a fuller and more satisfactory humanism. Indeed, what is lacking, in Canada, as well as in other industrialized countries, is the interest for true human values, as a means to develop an intelligent and moral culture.
I mentioned, among other things, the national film board and the Canada Council, which look after a number of artistic fields, and which do not receive large enough grants from the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, I think that, in addition to town planning, we should have road planning.
Moreover, there are the fields of medical research and amateur sport, the development of international and interprovincial games, physical culture and national parks, which the Canadian government should look after to its heart's content, if it wants to make a real contribution to the welfare of our Canadian citizens. As long as nothing is done to develop the fields I mentioned a while ago, including national parks, arts and sports, Canadians will remain incomplete, they will be men who live at the rhythm of the 20th century, at the speed of machines, men who leave industry in increasing number because they are displaced by automation.
The services of Canadians are less and less required in the field of sales. Let us find a place for them. Let us train them to find an interest in those things which can make life more agreeable; let us develop those fields I mentioned a while ago.
Mr. Chairman, I realize that the ideas I have just put forward concerning such development at a greater speed may seem out of order at this time and place. However, I feel that, quite to the contrary, such development is necessary and that such ideas must be advocated if we truly wish Canada to develop in all fields of endeavour.

I do not think this opportunity should be allowed to pass without a word or two being said about the so-called program of the Liberal government in respect to employment, and programs which would provide jobs for the Canadian people, as promised at the time of the last election campaign. The government has failed to implement this promise. It has implemented no program of its own; it has duplicated the programs of the previous government and, where there has not been duplication progress has been made only in those areas where progress was already well under way under the previous administration.

In a pamphlet which I hold in my hand entitled "The Policies of the Liberal Government" issued at the time of the 1963 general election we find on page 10 of this informative little document a heading: "Full Employment and Finances". The first thing the Liberal party was going to do was to set up a national economic council. Then we find the following promise made to the people of Canada-a promise which the government has failed to fulfil and one which I doubt very much they can fulfil. I quote:
Liberal action for new industry for community and area development will be planned together to create the 250,000 new jobs we need every year in order to achieve full employment and job security for a growing population.
I want to say a word about that promise which was so rampantly made across this country during the last election campaign. The Liberal party pledged itself to provide a quarter of a million new jobs each year. This was an extremely deceitful promise-deceitful because the party which made it knew at the time that the annual growth of new employment opportunities in this country amounts to roughly 250,000 per year; if this were not the case, the unemployment figures today would be astronomical rather than being so close to the figures of last year and the year before. The Liberal party went across this country promising that this gross unemployment which afflicted the Canadian people would be solved by 60 days of forceful action-60 days in which a new economic foundation was to be laid in this country so as to provide the new jobs which would make the Canadian people fat and happy. A turkey in every fridge and a Cadillac in every garage- that was the gist of the promises made by the Liberal party.
I ask the government this: When does it intend to take action on this plan to reestablish the national economy? Are we to expect the kind of action we got from the Minister of Finance when he presented his first budget? This expert, the Minister of Finance, has published two books in which he has described the problems of the Canadian economy and assessed the economic prospects before us, yet he has not put forward any new economic policies. He has contented himself by extending the policies of the previous government which were already in existence. Anything new which he has proposed has been withdrawn as unacceptable to industry, business, or international neighbourliness.

With our severe winters, and our general economic set-up, we'll always have a considerable body of jobless.

People who say we are going to eliminate unemployment simply don't know the country.
Yet remember when those opposite were on this side of the house, in opposition, how they decried the rate of unemployment in this country? Now, apparently, it is all right; now apparently, the fact that we have only-
It is respectable.

It is respectable, now they are on the government benches; all of a sudden it has become respectable. The Minister of Finance said, too, concerning unemployment, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star of January 24, 1962:
This does not need to happen. In fact, it is inexcusable.
I will go along with the Minister of Finance on that. When is he going to do something about it? When is the government going to do something about those myriads of dazzling promises that were made to the Canadian people in order deceitfully to obtain their votes during the last campaign? I have in my hand a pamphlet-as a matter of fact I have a whole file full of pamphlets-published by the Liberal party during the last election campaign. This particular one is entitled, "Pay and conditions on the job. The answer". The Liberals had all the answers during the last election campaign; there was no problem they could not solve, none whatsoever. Here is what they said in this pamphlet with regard to unemployment insurance. You remember sir, how the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the then member for Laurier, when they were on this side of the house

drove this question of unemployment insurance into the ground; they milked it for all it was worth. They said in the last campaign, "As soon as we form the government, we will fix everything up".
We never said that.
I heard a member say, "We never said that." The hon. member should come into the chamber, if he wants to make an interjection, and identify himself. I think it was the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
No, that is not his constituency; it is Windsor Castle.

The hon. member for Lotbiniere says they never made that promise. He does not seem to be familiar with his own propaganda. Let me read this to him:
The main Liberal policy for unemployment is to cure it.
When? When are they going to cure unemployment, the unemployment they said was so rife and which is not much better today? The pamphlet goes on to say:
In the Liberal view, the opportunity to work is a right of every Canadian.
What a magnificent statement that is; and yet what a deceitful statement to make when the imputation is that every Canadian has a right to work. They said, "We are the only people, if you elect us, who can bring it about." What deceit. The pamphlet goes on:
The heavy chronic unemployment of the past few years has made the unemployment insurance fund unsound.
I ask the hon. member for Lotbiniere to listen very carefully here:
A new Liberal government, with policies of economic growth, will restore the fund and enable it to function again for its proper purpose, which is to provide protection against short term and occasional unemployment.
That was the promise, and yet the fund is in the same shape today as it was when we were in office. When are the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour going to do something about this? What has happened to the recommendations of the Gill commission? When is something going to be done about implementing those recommendations? When are the criticisms of the now Secretary of State for External Affairs and the then member for Laurier going to receive the attention of the government? If it was such a dreadful thing in the days when those who now occupy the treasury benches were sitting on this side of the house, why is it not just as dreadful today? The benefits of genuine unemployment insurance will be extended to the widest possible coverage.
Here is another promise, for the benefit of the member for Lotbiniere, whose constituents I am sure cast a great many of their votes on the basis of these promises which have not been fulfilled.

False promises; deceitful promises-because the Canadian people were misled. As the Prime Minister, the leader of the party to which he belongs, said in a speech during the election campaign, "Gross deceit of the Canadian electorate". That is what these promises are, these unfulfilled promises.
This was part of our four year program.

A four year program, indeed. We were promised in Canada 60 days of blazing action. This government has been in office almost a year and a half and we have not even had an intimation that any program is going to be advanced, beyond the short term remedies announced by the Minister of Labour from time to time.

speechtext: All we got was a loused up budget.

That was the promise. When is it going to be implemented?
In fairness to all workers-

-a new Liberal government will be firm in preventing abuses of the insurance fund by people who are not genuinely without jobs.
When is this program going to commence? I think an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Province for September 3, 1963 has some bearing on the subject matter of the debate which has been opened by the hon. member for Ontario. This editorial says:

When the Liberals were in opposition in Ottawa they overlooked no opportunity to exaggerate the problem, even when it hurt Canada internally and externally.
That is so. You remember, sir, how they went across the country decrying the devaluation of the dollar. The Liberal party said that Canada was going to rack and ruin because the dollar had been devalued. That is to say, most of the Liberals said this. The Minister of Finance said it was a good thing that the dollar had been devalued; and the Minister of Trade and Commerce is able to report to the house that there has been an increase in our economy as a result of increased exports and the like. The reason for this is because the dollar was devalued; government members realize that now. As one hon. member suggested a moment ago, it is not that all of a sudden they have become respectable.
The editorial goes on:
It was an issue which might help to elect them.
I can remember what was the view on the devaluation of the dollar in one particular community in my constituency. The Liberal propaganda of that day to the Indian people in this community was this. They asked: What does the devaluation of the dollar mean? The Liberal machine went around to the Indian people and answered that question in this way: It means that when you take $1 into the beer parlour you will get one bottle of beer and 40 cents change. In other words, you do not get two bottles of beer. That is what they said, all the time knowing that devaluation was a good thing for the Canadian economy. As a result of devaluation the balance of tourist dollars in this country is on the credit side for the first time in Canada's history.
This editorial goes on to say:
In this narrow view victory, not principle or national welfare, seemed to be the guiding star.
And so it was.
It is probably safe to say that at no time, not even when unemployment was reported to be at its worst, was it ever as bad as the gloomsters made out. What is more, the depression talk never created a single job. In fact it probably did the opposite by creating doubt about Canada's present and future.
Investors were discouraged. Manufacturers changed their minds about establishing plants, and good immigrants were frightened and went elsewhere.
That was the sum product of the policy of campaigning which was evolved by the Liberal party during their last election campaign. They did not care about the harm

which was being done to the Canadian image abroad and at home. All they cared about was being elected. I think, sir, that they are going to have to chew over these promises which were made throughout the last election campaign. They are going to have them brought home to them with some force, and are going to have to admit that they were false promises, made merely for the purpose of riding into office on a horse of deceit, if I may put it in that way.
Another pamphlet says:
The government's job is to provide coherent policies based on long views of our national needs and welfare, not on temporary expedients.
Where has this program for jobs for the 45 year olds and over gone? How many houses have been built? How many people have been helped under the $500 winter building bonus? How many people have been helped by the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and construction machinery? Is this the program of the Liberal party for encouraging the growth of industry in this country? The Liberals went up and down the length and breadth of the country saying that they were going to reduce taxes. They were going to cut taxes and balance the budget. The first thing they did when they came into office was to increase taxes. If that is not deceit, then I do not know what is. The Canadian people were misled.

Disillusioned and fed up.

those interested in a problem which will soon begin to assume grave proportions in this country.
What about the young people of Canada? That sum was spent in two and a half years. I would ask the Minister of Labour, how much has been spent by his administration in the last fiscal year? The Liberal election campaign pledge to get the economy rolling at a fast enough clip to reduce unemployment and create one million new jobs by 1967 is foundering.
You bet your life, sir, it is foundering. They were going to cut taxes, set up all sorts of foundations for a new economy, balance the budget; all empty promises. What did the Prime Minister say during the campaign?
Many things.

As the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm points out, he said many things.
