Mr. Chairman-
Red Skelton.

-I hear my friend from Windsor calling me Red Skelton. As I told him before, I always appreciate these compliments. This afternoon I should like to say a few words with particular reference to labour relations. I just wish the Minister of Justice were here to hear them because they are in reference to our Liberal friend, Mr. Banks. If I may be personal for a few
[Mr. Nielsen. 1
moments, in 1938 I worked on a construction gang in the building of an airport. I was working my way through college at the time and I got 30 cents an hour on that job. At that time there were 300 to 400 men for each job and I learned to respect and have always respected since the right of men to organize into unions, to be paid fair wages, to work fair hours, to have a fair share of the national income and to be able to bargain with their entrepreneurs. If that association is to continue I believe it must continue under democracy as we know it within the rule of law.
My charge this afternoon, and it is a serious one, is that the government is making a mockery out of administration of justice as far as Hal Banks is concerned. I am sure that the people in the S.I.U., except the friends of Banks, and in other unions feel that a man like Banks has contributed nothing to the labour movement and nothing to the ability of labour to be able to negotiate with their entrepreneurs and obtain fair wages and fair working hours. In fact, he has done more to destroy their image across this country than any other individual.
On June 29 last the Supreme Court of Canada heard an appeal by Banks, which they dismissed, with the result that he had to serve a 30 day jail sentence for contempt of court. Today, more than three weeks later, Mr. Banks is at large. Why? I will try to answer that question in a few moments. Efforts this week to serve a writ of arrest on the deposed head of the S.I.U. ended in failure because Mr. Banks was nowhere to be found. The Minister of Justice does not know where he is and the Minister of Labour does not seem to know where he is. At least, they claim they do not know. The Prime Minister does not know where he is. Yet a radio station in Montreal knew his whereabouts. They say he is sunning himself at his cabin at Higgins beach. Yet the government does not know where he is.
Then, they say they will look into the matter. The Prime Minister says this is serious, and that he will give an answer tomorrow. It is like Alice in Wonderland with this government. There is never jam today, but always jam tomorrow.
Then, when tomorrow comes we have the parliamentary secretary answering because the Minister of Justice is in Edmonton. He says, well, really this is a provincial matter. I am going to suggest to the government that the radio station was called again, and what did they say? We have asked the govern-

ment questions on this but we cannot get any answers. We cannot find out whether it is the Department of Labour or the Department of Justice, but we are told now there are two federal agents-whether it is the R.C.M.P. or not, we do not know-working in conjunction with the United States authorities trying to ascertain whether Banks is at the beach and intends to stay there and flaunt the law of Canada. I know that under the British North America Act the administration of justice is under the attorney general of the province. However, the Minister of Justice in this country is the attorney general for Canada. If the attorney general of any one of the provinces is not fulfilling his duties and responsibilities, then it is up to the Minister of Justice or the attorney general to take up that responsibility that the other party may be shirking.
If the federal government says they have no responsibility, let me ask these questions. Why did they hire two crown counsel? Why did they have crown counsel recommend that charges should not only be laid against Banks but be laid against McLaughlin? We got this admission from the present government finally after asking question after question in reference to this matter. Then we were able to get action. Banks was tried, convicted and given five years. Why wasn't McLaughlin charged? What was the recommendation of the two counsel who were paid by the Department of Justice, not by the attorney general's branch of Quebec or Ontario, but by the Department of Justice? What was their recommendation with regard to this matter? Why was it not carried out? Why is Banks still flaunting the law?
One difference between Canada and the United States is that Canada has developed and continued the Anglo-Saxon system of law and, let us be frank about it, has adopted the laws of Great Britain. If Britain has exported anything or created anything in the commonwealth, she has created the rule of law and the attempt to bring decency to our kind of civilization. I say seriously to the minister that when the government makes a mockery out of justice, then they are blocking the rule of law and the whole democratic process breaks down. I ask you this: If we were dealing with a little coal miner from East Coulee, Alberta or Canmore, Alberta who had been charged and given five years, would he be running around this country? Would he be crossing the border into the United States?
What does the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration say in this regard? When I asked

The newspapers across this country, including the Calgary Herald, are asking why. This is what the Calgary Herald said:
Why was this man not arrested immediately following the supreme court ruling?
I will tell the Calgary Herald why, and I will tell the Ottawa Journal as well as the other newspapers who are asking these questions. The serious editors across the country are asking these questions. This procedure is making a mockery of justice.
If he can buy it, they all can buy it.

That is probably true. However, I come back to the point I made. What would have happened to the average citizen if he had been convicted? The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice says that he was found guilty of contempt, but that it was a civil matter. The lawyers on the other side know that the moment you get an order for contempt of court it at least becomes a quasi criminal matter. Banks is in contempt of one of the supreme courts of this country, and also the Supreme Court of Canada. Surely when a man is in contempt of one of the supreme courts of this country and also the Supreme Court of Canada, this is something which should be checked into.
When a man is out on $25,000 bail while he is supposed to be serving a five year term -as a Canadian he has every right to be on bail while waiting for his appeal-once he breaks his recognizance then he is supposed to be taken into custody. You will find plenty of cases outlining this situation and there are some good lawyers on the other side who realize this is the case. There are numerous cases to this effect, but I do not want to take the time to quote them this afternoon. There are numerous authorities

in Crankshaw's Criminal Code to the effect that where a man is out on bail and commits another criminal offence, he is immediately arrested. This is what should be happening to Mr. Banks today. The reason I say it is not happening is that basically he is a friend of this government.
Why do I say that? I think it was last fall or some time earlier when the Leader of the Opposition was talking about this particular matter. He pointed out Banks' record, a list as long as your arm. He pointed out that Banks was brought over and given a special landing permit. This was done with the consent of the present Minister of Justice, a former minister of citizenship and immigration, and he was brought over because he was a friend of this government. This is the reason we are not getting the administration of justice in this country.
The newspaper asks, "Why has his apprehension been subjected to such an unwarranted delay?" Then, this newspaper article continues:
If an ordinary citizen found himself in similar circumstances, would he not be thrown into jail forthwith?
I will answer, yes.
In the period which has elapsed since the publication of the Norris commission report on great lakes violence, a report in which Mr. Banks was condemned as a vicious labour hoodlum, officialdom has displayed a curiously pussy-footed attitude In dealing with this matter.
You are pussy-footing because he is a friend of your government. Let us get him in jail where he belongs.
Oh, oh.

They laugh over on that side. I do not believe the citizens of this country are laughing. Even the important newspapers in this country are not laughing, because the minister is making a mockery of the administration of justice in relation to this matter. I continue to quote from the article:
There was a delay in implementing Mr. Justice T. G. Norris' recommendations that Mr. Banks be removed from his post as head of the S.I.U.
Perhaps Mr. Banks is still running the trustees. Perhaps Mr. Banks is still really the head of the S.I.U. However, he would not be if the government would accept its responsibility for administering justice.
Last autumn, the federal government stalled for 13 days before ordering execution of a warrant sworn out for Mr. Banks' arrest.
Let us deal with that for a moment. Hon. Mr. Chevrier, for whom I have a great

deal of respect, was then minister of justice. I asked him why he failed to execute the warrant for the arrest of Mr. Banks. He was ready to pick him up when he came down here with the S.I.U. They carried banners displaying the names of various constituencies, but they did not even know that some of the constituencies were west of the great lakes. On that occasion Mr. Banks drove a great big white Cadillac. This was the friend of this government. This man is out, flaunting the law and making a mockery out of the administration of justice. You delayed for 13 days.
If there were a warrant out for the arrest of any of you people, do you think you would be given 13 days standing around on parliament hill? Would any other citizen be given 13 days? Of course not. Well, if I were a Liberal friend I might.
It should be noted also that Mr. Banks was sentenced on May 1 to five years in penitentiary for conspiring to injure a rival union leader. He was granted bail, pending appeal on this conviction. In view of the gravity of this offence and in view of the fact that Mr. Banks is currently awaiting another trial on a similar charge, it was surely incumbent on the police to keep close tabs on his whereabouts....
Mr. Banks' current game of hide and seek with the law is acquiring the dubious characteristics of a Keystone Cop comedy.
That is what the Calgary Herald said, and I agree with it even though it is pretty proLiberal these days. It also said:
It is also making a mockery of Canadian justice.
Let us think about this for a few moments. We had the Norris report. We had to interrogate and press the government to get this man charged. Then we had to press the government to get him arrested. Finally he was tried and found guilty but the government can take no comfort in that. Unless the voices of the opposition had not spoken up day after day he would not have been charged.

speechtext:
On a question of privilege; the facts, as I say, arose in 1957. They were known to the former government. The Norris commission was not established until
1961.	Why did the former government stall?

Well I say the facts and the commission's recommendation were not brought before the house until a Liberal government was in office. I think the parliamentary secretary will go along with that, but assuming for a few moments that the parliamentary secretary is correct and that the Conservative government was dilatory, is that any excuse for the conduct going on now? You are the men of decision; you are the people of the new era.
I say to the parliamentary secretary that I question whether he believes that what he said the other day in the house is correct according to the law. I question whether today, upon reflection, he agrees that the matter is a civil one and the government and the Minister of Justice can do nothing about it. I say to him there is a responsibility on the government. He knows there is a responsibility; everyone knows there is a responsibility, but the government is shelving that responsibility.
Again I ask the simple question, would this occur if it had been another citizen. I say it would not. There is the history of it. This man was charged and found guilty and afterwards he flaunted the order with respect to contempt of court. I say there is a duty and a responsibility on the government to arrest this man and see that justice is done.
Let us look for a few moments at the law so far as bail is concerned. There has been a lot said about it, and I refer the parliamentary secretary to Canadian Criminal Cases volume 47, 1926-27. Except for a few changes in the interim the law of bail has not been altered. I wish to read from page 6 of this volume, from an article written by Eric Armour, K.C., at that time crown attorney in Toronto, and I am sure this will impress the parliamentary secretary because that is where he practised law before he became a distinguished parliamentary secretary.
Cash Bail: A justice of the peace as a substitute for bail may take a sum of money as a deposit.. .and this is so in respect of bearer bonds or other negotiable securities. But it is a matter entirely in his discretion and he may accept or refuse cash bail as he deems best. A deposit of a sum of money can be required

when a witness without means is bound over to give evidence...
There are, however, practical objections to cash bail.
What are they? I want to pause there for a few moments. Counsel hired by the government were competent counsel and I am sure they would have recommended that this man should have been placed on a proper recognizance, so that he could not move across a border to go sunning himself when he had been found guilty of the charge, and was in contempt of the court.
To accept from the prisoner himself, cash or securities for bail is often, in effect, to permit him to purchase his freedom-
That is the charge I make. This man has purchased his freedom and has done so at the hands of the Liberal government. You have made a mockery of justice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I point out that the issuing or granting of bail is entirely within the discretion of the chief justice of the province of Quebec and it is a patent falsehood to say the bail is purchased from the Liberal government. Bail in this case is cash bail as set in proper exercise of judicial discretion by the chief justice of the province, and if the terms of the bail are not suitable to the hon. member he may very well criticize the judge's discretion; but it is quite improper to criticize the government in that regard.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to see you give the parliamentary secretary a good hand. He deserves a good hand for that remark, but he has missed my point. Judges make this decision and I am not criticizing the court for granting bail, but the parliamentary secretary knows as well as I do-he is not that naive-that crown counsel is the man who suggests the terms and conditions of the bail and the justice, the trial judge or the magistrate, goes along with that-
Oh, oh.

-and sometimes the defence counsel. It is a matter of open discussion. I notice hon. members opposite are trying to say there is something wrong with that, but they know as well as I do that crown counsel's suggestion is listened to very carefully because he has the man's record at hand and knows the character of the man. It is one of those considerations which judges take into consideration in exercising discretion as to whether they are going to

Interim Supply
grant bail or not, and I say to the government in that regard you did not perform your proper function. Did your crown counsel recommend cash bail, and if so, why?
When there are no sureties financially interested in seeing that the prisoner will answer the charge, and who, if they have doubts about it, can render him into custody, the chances of the accused appearing to stand trial are very greatly lessened.
We know what kind of man this is. He was a gangster when he was permitted to come here. He was a gangster after he came here, and he is still at large. That is the charge I make.
Let us take a look at what should have been in the recognizance bond. Whether it happened in Quebec, Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan or B.C., the criminal law is in the Criminal Code. You know, Mr. Chairman, it is rather unusual that when this man made out his application for immigration purposes that line, "Have you been found guilty of a crime" was left out and forgotten. I wonder, was it the same reason that led to this recognizance stipulation being forgotten. I invite the parliamentary secretary to give some serious thought to that.
I quote now from Crankshaw's Criminal Code of Canada, seventh edition, 1959, at page 1289.

1959, yes, that is the date. I always like to be interrupted by the hon. member for Windsor Castle. This is the recognizance form:
Now, therefore, the condition of the above written recognizance is that (if the accused appears at that court, or if, having re-elected under Part XVI, he appears before the presiding judge at the time and place fixed for his trial) and takes his trial on the indictment that is found against him and does not depart the said court without leave-
What does that mean? I know the parliamentary secretary is well aware what it means. "The said court" is the court which has jurisdiction. I say Banks should not be leaving the province of Quebec. That should have been part of his bond. If not, it was the duty of those responsible for the administration of justice to ascertain why, particularly after he had been condemned not only by the trial court in that province but by the supreme court. Surely, that makes sense.
Let us look at what some of the authorities say, as far as bail is concerned. As reported at page 1128 of the same volume, a man is charged with trafficking in narcotic drugs and bail is set at $20,000. When the case comes up, the accused fails to appear. Either on
(Mr. Woolliams.]
this charge, or on a charge precisely similar, the bail was cancelled. I say this is what should happen in this particular case. I say, too, that this matter should be discussed with the United States authorities and Banks should be brought back. I am certain they do not want to harbour Mr. Banks and that they would be glad to get rid of him. They do not want him down there, because when he was down there he had a criminal record "that long" anyway. Why was he brought to this country and why did this government allow this man to be free for 13 days when there was a warrant out for his arrest? Why did they not pick him up? These are questions which should be answered, but the government cannot answer them.
This affair has made a mockery out of the administration of justice. Not only is it bad in reference to Banks but it is bad in reference to the administration of the law generally. In this country we have respect for the law and this is one of the things which makes Canada respected all over the world. If we allow these things to go on we shall not only bring into disrepute the rule of law but we shall undermine the appreciation of the people for democracy and lessen the image of Canada abroad. All the newspapers are asking why these things have happened. I ask these questions, too. Did this man contribute to the Liberal party during the elections? Was he a friend of Mr. Harris, the former minister of finance? Was he a friend of the Minister of Transport? You know what the Minister of Transport said when the Leader of the Opposition was speaking? He said: "I don't turn my back on friends". I say: Turn your back on this friend; bring him to Canada and let him face the law in the same way as others. Put this hoodlum behind bars; protect labour and its organizations and maintain respect for the rule of law in this country.

There are a number of questions which naturally arise. I do not intend to follow my hon. friend from Bow River in going into particulars regarding Mr. Banks. I have dealt with that subject on previous occasions. I have indicated he was a coddled pet of the Liberal party throughout the years. However, the hon. member for Rosedale was in disagreement with some statements made by the hon. member for Bow River so I think I should like to quote a newspaper which he holds in great respect and which has an equal regard for him. I refer to the Toronto Daily Star. An editorial

in that paper, referring to the Liberal party and its position on this matter, states:
Admittedly his government-
-that is, the government of the present Prime Minister-
-has been patient with S.I.TJ. president Hal Banks, a sort of Liberal protege, ever since he arrived in Canada, criminal record and all, in 1949.
Then it goes on to say, among other things:
What was happened so far is not a pay-off; it looks more like a sell-out-a new "sweetheart deal" between Banks and the government.
I think that is pretty potent and cogent and I will say no more in that regard, except-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman state the date of that editorial?

Yes. October 26, 1963. And the title, so that the hon. gentleman may be fully informed, is "Pay Off or Sell Out, Mr. Pearson?". I waited for that question. It is always the last question that gets a lawyer into difficulty, as the young and hon. gentleman will learn when his practice has been extended by the experience of years.
Indeed, when I think of the complete farce in connection with Banks leaving Canada, going about his happy way after his arrest on a charge of contempt of court, confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada, and blithely going abroad to breathe the salubrious atmosphere of freedom which comes to those who can break the law with impunity, as he has done throughout the years, it is difficult to know precisely what ought to be said. The hon. member for Rosedale asked why the government did not do something about it during the period between 1957 and 1962. It was simply because we were unable to deport this man, the government of my predecessor in office having confirmed him as a Canadian resident, approved of his illegal entry, as it was, and given him a status which prevented his being put out of Canada as he should have been. As they go to search for him, it is strange, but a limerick comes to my mind which, no doubt, is known to many hon. members:
As I was going up the stair
I met a man who wasn't there.
He wasn't there again today;
I wish that man would stay away!
And it applies completely to what has happened in connection with Banks.
However, it is not of that I intend to speak today. I intend to speak of the degree to which this man still dominates the S.I.U. Despite his conviction-now before the courts

by way of appeal, and I make no observation on it for that reason-this man is still dominating the affairs of the S.I.U. today. In his place is Leonard McLaughlin. Read what Mr. Justice Norris had to say about McLaughlin-* the tool, the operative, for Banks. But now, as the hon. member for Port Arthur said this afternoon, we find that this individual whose record was one which desecrated the decencies, found by Mr. Justice Norris to have been disreputable in his conduct, discharges in the S.I.U. today the responsibilities of president of that union and does so with the approval of the maritime trustees; otherwise he could not hold the position he does. Banks, no longer the titular head, is the effective head, if this means anything Mr. McLaughlin intends to appoint, or has already appointed, to the union's executive six men who had previously held key positions in the Banks regime.
The Globe and Mail dealt with this in an editorial and, again, if the hon. gentleman wants to read it and bring himself up to date, it is dated May 4, 1964. It seems strange that we could have acted as a parliament-and, we believed, effectively-in fulfilling a request of the government to approve of a maritime trusteeship board. In the intervening months, we have had reports, and I intend to refer to those reports.
Parliament day by day has been denied information, the minister occupying a position of simply being, as it were, an in-between and failing to have a direct and solid opinion on this question. I listened to him the other day. I thought he had agreed that he would recommend to the trustees that they should report to parliament, that they should come before a parliamentary committee. This afternoon there were revelations made by the hon. member for Port Arthur. He recommended Mr. Millard, and that hon. member said today he had reason to be disappointed with that recommendation. He indicated that in so far as the chairman is concerned and the other members of the board, they did little, the responsibility apparently falling on Mr. Millard. The Minister of Labour will be able to reply to the hon. member for Port Arthur in that connection.
But parliament has the right to know what is going on. We cannot get it from the minister. We ask him for information, and his answer is that the matter will be brought to the attention of the trustees. Naturally they do not want to appear before a committee of parliament. Somebody today said that if they appeared before a committee, it might weaken

their position in their work. That is not what they fear. That is not what I fear. I believe that parliament has a right to know what is going on. How are we going to weaken the administration of a board by bringing them before parliament and asking certain questions? I thought the Minister of Labour agreed with hon. members-I think generally, in all parts of the house-that this board should appear before a committee of parliament. I thought he agreed last week, but on Friday he gave this answer, as reported at page 5926 of Hansard, to a question by me. I asked:
May I ask a supplementary question. I wanted to ask the Minister of Labour, in his communication with the trustees did he add his personal request that they should now be willing to appear before the committee? What did he mean when he said "We will meet at an early date"? Does that mean he is going to meet with them?

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped it might be possible to have a discussion on this point with the chairman of the board of trustees either on Monday or later next week.
Why wait until Monday; why wait until later this week? Are there no telephones; is there no other communication than meeting together? This is a matter that has been before parliament on a number of occasions and members have asked for, have demanded, their right and parliament's right to know what is going on here-because certainly there are things that require explanation, with regard to which parliament has the right to information. But said the Minister of Labour:
However, the chairman had made arrangements to be on the west coast. Just as soon as he comes back we will have a meeting to discuss the particular point raised by my hon. friend. At that time I hope I will be in a position to indicate my views as to the desirability or otherwise of an appearance before the committee.
Up until Friday I believed the minister was himself convinced that this board of trustees should appear before a committee of parliament. That was the indication he gave to the house on more than one occasion; and yet on Friday he added these significant words, "my views as to the desirability or otherwise". In other words, he retraced his steps. The undertaking of a day or so before, which was clear and apparent to anyone who listened to his words, was dissipated and removed by those additional words. Why should they not come before a committee of parliament? What is the reason? There are a great many questions that have to be answered.
There will be the question of Mr. McLaughlin. Just imagine him, sitting in as the grand mogul of the S.I.U. This is the man who was the pawn of Banks, the man who carried out Banks' brutalities or, rather, his tyrannical

directions. That was his position; he was Banks' trusted operator. He is now the head of the S.I.U.; if not in law then certainly in fact. Would the minister say whether this person has suddenly become the epitome of all goodness? Has the record of several years as the factotum of Mr. Banks all been erased? Has purity taken the place of the wrongdoing of those years? The minister laughs. That is his attitude, laughing at this; laughing at a situation in having a man as the head of the
S.I.U., who still operates-whether they can find it or not-the "do not ship" list. The hon. member from the N.D.P. referred to this matter again today. He still operates this list. Men get in touch with me and say, "We cannot get positions; we are on the 'do not ship' list". We asked for the "do not ship" list and the minister said there is not any such list.
Judge Wagner of Montreal, a man who has earned a national reputation for justice and its administration, made unflattering references to Leonard McLaughlin. Why should this man, who favoured Banks-that was the word used in his evidence, apparently-be elevated to the top position? The minister will say, "Oh, we let the unions operate as they will and choose whom they will, and in the ordinary role of progression upwards, being the vice president he would naturally fill the position vacated by Banks". That is not what the Canadian people want. They want free labour removed from any suggestion of domination by the Banks gang. I thought the minister would have impressed upon the trustees the fact that members in all parts of this house-if I know anything about it-contend that McLaughlin is unacceptable. But he is going to serve. What about the C.L.C.? The leaders of the Canadian Labour Congress warned, as far back as April 20, that "democracy cannot be achieved in the seafarers' international union of Canada until the present officers of the S.I.U. are ousted".
Three months ago Mr. Jodoin said in an interview that that statement stands as congress policy, although it was written before the government's marine union trustees deposed S.I.U. president Hal Banks. I should like the minister to tell the committee when McLaughlin changed his spots; it would be very interesting to know. He was a leopard in labour relations in the S.I.U. Has he now changed? If he has it speaks volumes for the beneficient influence of the Minister of Labour. What questions could be asked. What would we like to know.

Let us look back to the Norris commission report. The Norris commission spent a year hearing hundreds of witnesses and taking thousands of pages of evidence. They dealt with the S.I.U. and its ramifications. They dealt with Hal Banks' ruthless rise to power. They dealt with the means whereby he maintained absolute power and exercised his chilling authority over democratic and labour processes. The evidence indicated the brutal authoritarianism of and the part played by Leonard McLaughlin. Does the minister say that I am overstating the record as far as McLaughlin is concerned? Justice Norris said, as reported at page 169 of his report:
His subservience to and support of Banks under all circumstances was demonstrated at an early stage.
Mr. Justice Norris suggests that McLaughlin's activities should be investigated along with Banks' with a view to laying conspiracy charges. Now the man against whom the recommendation was made that a conspiracy charge should be considered is in the driver's seat. What manner of contempt for parliament is this? What was the reason for setting up the commission? The recommendation by Mr. Justice Norris was to bring about the assurance of democracy in the union. What has been done in that connection? I want the minister to tell the committee what has been done. Certainly Banks' flunkey, McLaughlin, has been given the position which Banks occupied. Judge Wagner remarked how McLaughlin leaned to Banks. Cannot you see him sitting there in that position while Banks travels abroad and enjoys the vacation of which some of us dream, not abroad but in our own country? How these men must laugh. Do you mean to tell me, Mr. Chairman, that the man who for 13 years had no other function which is apparent on the record than to carry out the orders of Hal Banks has suddenly become the reverse of what he was under the tutelage of Banks over a period of time? He is the man who owed his position and his salary to Banks; the man who never scrupled to do Banks' bidding.
The Norris report, as all of us agreed, unfolded a record page by page of violence and brutality. Where was McLaughlin when the beatings were going on? Judge Norris said of him that McLaughlin's greatest asset was his adeptness-and I quote-"at setting up the farce of democracy in the union". The man who was adept at setting up the farce of democracy in the union is the chosen instrument for bringing about an assurance of democracy which is one of the major tasks 20220-382

suggested by Justice Norris. I say that in the interests of the freedom of labour in this land, in the interests of equality under the law and in the interests of parliamentary supremacy these trustees must be summoned before parliament to give their evidence and be cross-examined.
What about Paul Hall? We have not yet been told about the arrangement made by Paul Hall. The maritime trades department of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. was operated by Banks and Paul Hall, who is the president of the
5.1.	U. in the United States. Then there was the L.I.A. which was formerly run by Tony Anastasia, but which is now operated by Mr. Gleason who paid a visit to Montreal last year. Then there is also the teamsters union, and only a couple of days ago Mr. Hoffa added to the sum total of his convictions.
They are racketeers. We are not going to have this sort of thing in Canada. Can we be assured that we will not have it by having the McLaughlins head the S.I.U.? After the minister has spoken I hope I will be able to have a later opportunity to deal with any matters he might raise and any answers he gives. Because the record is in the Norris report.
Among the questions which might be asked are: What is McLaughlin's position? Is he still running the union? Whose orders is he carrying out? Are they the orders of the trustees, or Hal Banks, or Paul Hall? How much control has Paul Hall, president of the
5.1.	U. in the United States, over the S.I.U. in Canada? What financial contributions are being made now by the S.I.U. to the S.I.U. in the United States? We should like to find out whether an agreement was reached with Paul Hall on that question. We should like to find out whether Canadian sailors are still being forced to pay contributions which come into Paul Hall's hands in order to hold down jobs. Surely we have the right to this information.
We should like to have the opportunity to examine these trustees regarding the "do not ship" lists. We should like to find out how many new contracts have been negotiated by the seamen of the S.I.U. We should like know whether these contracts provide for a portable pension plan with a 20 per cent wage increase. We should like to hear from Mr. Millard, a man who has had a great record in Canadian public life and in union activities. What conversations and discussions have taken place between him and Leonard McLaughlin?

There is something else we would like to find out. On March 10 the board of trustees made a report in which they said:
The trustees have felt that.. .the removal and replacement of any officer of any union-
That included Banks.
-should be effected, whenever this is necessary, by persons and processes in the trade union movement itself.
When that report was made on March 10 Banks was still in office. What happened between March 10 and March 18 when the board of trustees decided to remove Banks? These are just some of the questions that naturally arise. Let us consider the trustees' report further. Here are some questions. They say in their report:
They also decided to interfere as little as possible with the affairs of the unions consistent with carrying out the duties of the trustees under the act.
I doubt whether or not that was in the contemplation of parliament. They were given great power in order to preserve free unionism in Canada. They went on to say in their report:
Should anything be found in the course of this investigation-
-of the financial and other aspects of the unions under trusteeship-
-that showed the conduct of a union officer or officers to be inconsistent with his or their remaining in office, it was agreed appropriate steps, as provided in the legislation, would be taken.
We would like to know what was found as a result of this investigation because they went on to say:
In the meantime, it was agreed that the officers would continue to administer the unions subject to the control of the trustees as provided by he act.
We would like to hear about the discussions between Mr. Hall and the trustees. We would like to be able to look into the question of whether or not there was in fact any arrangement made between them. In the report of last March this item appears:
An insurance company has been asked to review the seafarers' international union welfare plan.
What has happened? What was found as a result of that review? The report goes on to state:
Preliminary discussions indicate that more data will be needed than are at present available before clear answers can be obtained as to the relative merits of the present plan and alternatives to it. A decision has not yet been made as to whether or not the expense of collecting these data should be incurred.

Was there an investigation? We would like to know. We would like to know what was found as a result of the examination made by a firm of chartered accountants retained in October, 1963 to advise the trustees as to control and investigation of the financial affairs of the unions. We would also like to find out what explanation was given for the shortage of $4,965.01 in the total funds available compared with the total liabilities as set out on page 5. We were told that all of these things were being considered and we would like to know what has been done, with these recommendations extant and such important matters to be looked into as Hal Banks' travels. The accountants were instructed to find and train someone to carry out the program so devised. I quote the words of the report:
They were Instructed to do so, and were also asked to prepare a set of rules to cover expense account entitlement.
What was done in that regard? After all, the record was that whatever Banks wanted, Banks got. However large the expenditure it was approved by him and on more than one occasion exorbitant, inexcusable and unjustifiable amounts were paid. What about these investigations as to the books of the union regarding the use of the building corporation's property? The report stated:
No separate books of account are kept by the corporation. The bookkeeper will be instructed to keep records that will permit a more detailed accounting for future periods.
We want to know what was done. Parliament has no information. All we know is that some ephemeral plan was evolved, some potential operation was determined on. What has been done? While all these plans are made Banks travels, and McLaughlin sits in a position of responsibility.
What about the list of addresses of the seamen? It was found that was out of date and for other reasons inaccurate and would have to be corrected. What has been done in that connection? There are so many questions here involving financial matters, adjustment of disputes and prevention of possible work stoppages. These have required the issuance of special instructions. We would like to know what has happened. The board went on to say:
In the hope of finding a permanent solution to the problems which gave rise to the trusteeship, the trustees have endeavoured to ascertain the basic causes of, and to devise remedies for, the conditions which the statute calls upon them to correct.
What has been done? Somebody said something today about parliament being in disre-

pute. I do not belong to that school. If you will read Hansard you will find that all through the years members have said how different parliament was in the grand old days of the past. That does not mean that changes do not have to take place; but parliament cannot act without information and parliament has a right to know what is taking place here.
The trustees were to consider such matters as hiring halls, collection of union dues and assessments, the appointment of officials to review discharges of seamen, the training and certification of personnel. What has been done? The trustees also stated:
In the course of their inquiries the trustees have been examining the hiring methods used in other countries in the hope that their solution to somewhat similar problems might be helpful in Canada.
We want to know what has happened. Certainly none of these things is secret. How can information of this kind not be beneficial? I have never yet known a parliament to operate effectively blindfolded. Let us shine the searchlight into the recesses of the S.I.U. The only way we can do so is by having the trustees come before us.
With regard to McLaughlin and other responsible officers the report contains the following:
The trustees have felt that, if at all possible, the removal and replacement of any officer of any union should be effected, whenever this is necessary, by persons and processes in the trade union movement itself. Consequently, they have concluded that every effort should be made to induce responsible officers of the trade union movement to make changes where they are required.
Will anybody tell me that McLaughlin is responsible? He is powerful. What changes have taken place in the S.I.U. since the month of March? Then the trustees go on to say:
Should such efforts fail, or not be employed or if...it appears to the trustees that the past or present conduct of a union officer makes it advisable in the interests of the future conduct of union affairs to remove him, or that the removal of an officer is in the interests of the welfare of Canada, he will, of course, be removed.
Do you notice the word "past", the past conduct of a union officer? I ask the minister this question: What about the past conduct of the man who today parades as the chief of the S.I.U.?
Mr. Justice Norris can be consulted if anybody wants an answer to that.
Now, sir, these are the questions that we want to have answered. It may be inconvenient for the trustees, for after all none of us 20220-3821

Then, this article deals with the question of collective bargaining agreements, and I am not going into that. On April 4 the press reported that a deal had been made between the trustees and Paul Hall, president of the

We get the brush-off, and that is not unusual in the last few weeks. We have had the brush-off several times by the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Agriculture. We cannot get any information. This report is dated March 24, 1964. What were those things? Surely no board set up by parliament should operate in that way, which denies parliament information. We were told, at the time the bill was before the house that there would be a formal report once a year, and we accepted that. The minister said he was sure interim reports would be made available under all reasonable circumstances.
Now then, I could go on and ask various other questions. I mentioned a moment ago the question of pensions and new contract demands. This is on April 13, and I quote from the article:

New contract demands for Canadian seamen under the maritime union trustees board will provide for a portable pension plan and a possible 20 per cent wage increase, it was learned here on the week end. ...
Notification has also gone out to 42 shipping companies that the S.I.U. intends to open contract negotiations some time in May.
What has been done? These, and many other questions, should be answered. This parliament cannot, must not and dare not allow itself to be flouted. The former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario, today expressed his view, as has the hon. member for Bow River. I had hoped that the other day the minister was in agreement when he expressed himself on this question of the trustees appearing before a committee of the house. However, he made it very clear that parliament would not know what his personal views were in this regard. No doubt when he speaks he will be able to clarify these things. However there is one thing upon which clarification is necessary, and that is the right of parliament to this information, because Banks' visit abroad and McLaughlin's appointment reveal the kind of hanky-panky that is being played with responsible unionism.
I will go no farther than that now. The failure to recognize that parliament has rights, that the rights of the people have been interfered with and trampled on as they were by Banks and McLaughlin, is an important matter.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the Chair.

I wish to use this occasion when we are assaulting the Minister of Labour to make a few comments, some of them on matters which were brought up this afternoon, but many of them on matters which are new. All of them relate to fields which come under the minister's jurisdiction.
I wish to point out that for backbenchers like myself this is the first opportunity we have had in the second session of the twenty sixth parliament to discuss anything relating to the Department of Labour apart from occasional opportunities through questions on the orders of the day. The reason for this situation is that the Minister of Labour has either chosen not to introduce his estimates or else he cannot convince his colleagues that they should take any kind of priority. Perhaps it is because the hon. gentleman is afraid to account for what has been going on, particularly in relation to the maritime trusteeship. At any rate, it becomes important for someone like myself to put on record at this particular juncture a few remarks with regard to the Department of Labour.
I want to begin by making a public confession. I, like many other members, feel I was "conned" into voting for a trusteeship last fall. I did so then, but I am not so sure I would now. In fact, I am practically certain I would not vote to impose a trusteeship on unions in Canada if the same issues were to come before this house again. It runs against my grain, anyway; but we in this house were impressed at the time by the heinous offences which had been committed by Mr. Banks and Mr. McLaughlin. The minister, and the ministry generally, said the imposition of a trusteeship was the only thing which could be done to clean up the union, though the measure left a bad taste in the mouth of any person who saw himself as a friend of organized labour. I was reluctant to vote for it at the time, and I was sorry I had done so. I would not vote that way again. What has happened in the interim is that the government, having introduced this legislation and appointed the trustees, has failed to carry out the spirit of the legislation and see to it

that these violent and gangsterish people were removed from the seafarers international union.
The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice can give all kinds of excuses, and so can the Minister of Labour. The fact of the matter is that Banks is sitting sunning himself at a sea resort in Maine while his minion, McLaughlin, is running the S.I.U. The charge has been made in this house that Mr. Banks was allowed to get across the border after arranging for this mere $25,000 bail. I say "mere" in the sense that, to hoodlums like Banks, $25,000 is not very much money. The charge was made in the house this afternoon by the hon. member for Bow River that the only reason Banks is free and at large is because the Liberal government chose to wink at his activities and that, in fact, the price of peace on the great lakes was that Banks be allowed, with tacit approval from the Liberal government, to cross the border into the United States to holiday in Maine, knowing that his front men were still running the S.I.U. If this is not true I do not know why the Minister of Labour does not get up and say it is not true. That is all he needs to do. If these charges are false then, surely, the minister should give the house a categorical denial. Otherwise, how can one explain what has been going on? I would be perfectly happy to resume my seat right now if the minister would get up and categorically deny that a deal was made between Paul Hall and the trustees appointed by parliament whereby Mr. McLaughlin would acquire the presidency of the
S.I.U. as the price of peace on the great lakes. If the minister is prepared to deny it, the issue would be ended as far as I am concerned. But how else can anyone in this house understand the events of the past few months in relation to this gangster Banks and the fact that as great a gangster though possibly a less accomplished one, is now in command of the union? I am sure many members on all sides of the house are sincerely sorry they voted in favour of a maritime trusteeship as they did last fall.
After these opening remarks I wish to refer briefly to a situation of which I am sure the minister is aware. It is one which, I believe, is a matter for deep concern. At the present time there is only one area in Canada where the working man has absolutely no labour legislation to protect him. That area, as hon. gentlemen may guess, is the Northwest Territories. At the present time there is no minimum wage law, no legislation guaranteeing annual vacations, no legislation with regard
Interim Supply
to hours of work, overtime, and so on. I think that it is properly the responsibility of the minister to take a hard look at this situation and give some leadership. I am asking him on behalf of the working men of the Northwest Territories to provide such leadership. I feel there must be labour legislation introduced quickly, and for two reasons. First, we have to protect the men who are already there, even though they may number only some 2,000 employees. In the second place, if we are ever to develop this part of the country it is essential that employers who come into the area and the employees who work for them should know what their rights and responsibilities are, and that these rights should be shored up by legislation.
Before anyone interrupts me, let me say I know perfectly well that labour legislation is a matter which properly falls within the jurisdiction of the territories council. But I know, also, that the council of the Northwest Territories is completely dominated by the federal government-that it is a nine man council to which the minister of northern affairs appoints five persons, and that nothing can go on in the council without his approval. So I do know that if, in the case, the minister of northern affairs wishes to do so, he can see to it that labour legislation is introduced at the next session of the territories council.
So far there has been one group and one group only pressing for even rudimentary labour legislation in Canada's north, and that is the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers who are very active in the north and in the Yukon. For the last three years in particular they have consistently approached the government, pointing out these areas of inadequacy and asking for action. Tonight I am asking the Minister of Labour if, through the excellent staff officers he has, he will take this whole matter under study.
I want to read from the final statement that was issued after a conference of the mine, mill and smelter workers at Whitehorse in August of 1962. They had men representing the various unions from all over, both in Yellowknife just prior to the 1962 election campaign and subsequently in the Yukon in August of the same year, and they Issued a statement of what they wanted. I just want to read this statement to the minister because in any other part of Canada this sort of thing was happening years ago. There is only this one remaining area with regard to which we have no legislation in this con-

nection. Here is the statement they issued after this conference:
As stated in the preamble, the inadequacy of the labour legislation in the Yukon, and the complete non-existence of labour legislation in the Northwest Territories make it imperative that a labour code be devised to meet the needs of workmen in the rapidly expanding economy of our northland.
Therefore, the union urges that an ordinance or labour code be enacted that will give workers in the north rights equal to those enjoyed by workmen in the other areas of our nation.
The union submits the following as minimum requirements for the formulation of such a labour code.
It will come as a shock to some people that this is all these men are asking for and that these things are not there:
(a)	Minimum wage.
(b)	Hours of work.
(c)	Overtime rates.
(d)	Minimum paid vacations.
<e) Paid statutory holidays.
(f) Guarantee of wages.
It surely must come as a shock to Canadians that the men who work in these areas do not have any of these guarantees; that it is only on the basis of whim or benevolence that a workman there gets these things. I suggest to the minister that it is up to him to give the leadership in this regard. He should call his officials in and tell them he is not satisfied that there should be a developing part of Canada-indeed, any part of Canada, no matter how small it is-where a workman does not even have a guaranteed holiday per year, does not have guaranteed hours of work, and has no minimum wage at all. In this regard these people are extremely unfortunate, particularly when this is an area that has in it so many Eskimo and Indian people and where it is up to the employer to decide whether or not he shall exploit the people who are working for him. I could read from other publications of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers. As I said before, this is the only agency that has consistently pressed for the protection of the rights of the workman in the north. Now I am lending my voice, on the first occasion I have had, really, to do this and am asking the minister if he will consider taking action in this regard.
I want to refer the minister very briefly to another little squabble that is going on in the north. It is little in one sense, and it is an important one in another. The minister is well aware of it because already he has intervened. I am referring to the difficulties we have encountered on the distant early warning line. I am not alone in speaking in

this connection in the house; the member of the New Democratic party for Winnipeg North Centre has also raised this question with the minister. The history of the problem I can state very quickly. As a result of the diminishing threat of manned bomber attack from Russia, the D.E.W. line, the distant early warning line, is being phased out. As a result of this, the employees who have served on the line are placed in an unfortunate position. This is not a pleasant kind of service for most of these men, to be thousands of miles away from their families, in complete isolation, not allowed to have their families on site with them; it is an artificial and unfortunate kind of living. None the less the pay is good and over the years the men have built up a tradition of service on the line.
As jobs became scarce, the Federal Electric Corporation, which operates the D.E.W. line for the United States air force, decided that this would be a good time to cut wages and increase the workload of the men; that because they had more applicants with D.E.W. line experience than they had positions, they could force men who had served for five, six, seven or eight years to take a 25 per cent cut in pay. What happened was that the international brotherhood of electrical workers went in and organized the men on the line, and in May of 1963 certification of local 2085 of the international brotherhood was granted by the Canadian government, this after many years of difficulty. Believe you me, Mr. Chairman, the Federal Electric Corporation did not make it easy for the international brotherhood to go in there and organize these men; they put every possible stumbling block in their way.
At any rate, in May of 1963 they were finally certified as the bargaining agent. The Federal Electric Corporation immediately appealed this decision and it took some months before a decision was finally handed down. The minister will recall answering a question on this matter in the house in March of this year. His answer can be found on page 1404 of Hansard. He there gives the facts of the case and says that the way is now clear for the men to bargain effectively for their rights. This question involves some 500 or 600 employees. I posed a question to him on that same day and asked whether he would look into a problem that had been suggested to me, namely that Canadians working on the distant early warning line were being paid substantially less than United States citizens, for doing identical jobs, being employed in the same category.

I asked the minister to look into this matter, and he promised he would do so.
I am hoping that maybe he will be able to give me an answer now; because what is happening is that this United States corporation is paying those persons who are American citizens substantially higher wages than they are paying Canadians in the same location, doing the same work, and at the same employment level. This is a situation that has gone on for some time. But the recent difficulties, the recent retrenchments in positions have exacerbated this problem; they have brought it to the fore now, and the men are completely unhappy. I am sure the minister can understand why Canadians and why the member of parliament who represents these men on the line should be pretty upset. Right now there are conciliation board hearings going on in Winnipeg to review some of these problems of the men on the distant early warning line. What has happened is that as a result of earlier intervention from the minister's office the Federal Electric Corporation were told they could not get away with reducing these wages; that they must hold the line until the matter could be studied; that they were not to just chop the pay of the men whom they did not want to hire. Therefore the Federal Electric Corporation right now is employing a bunch of manoeuvres to, in effect, accomplish the same thing. I want to tell the minister about that because it is something I feel his departmental officials should look into. For example, when they are told they must pay the same rate, let us say for a radar technician, or a rad-ician, as they are called on the line, what the company has been doing has been to set up a new grade of radician at a much lower rate, and to hire men at the lower category for the same job. Or they are doing things like removing all cooks from the site, and the chef, who of course is one step up from a cook and receives more pay, is now having to do all the cooking, baking, and so on, as well as clean up. That is another way of cutting their pay or making the senior officers do more menial tasks.
Another thing they are doing, which I should like the minister or his officials to note, is that they are bringing in a lot of temporary employees for terms of less than four months. If the minister is familiar with the distant early warning line he will realize that under Federal Electric regulations an employee who is in the employ of the company for less than four months is not eligible to join the union. Therefore they are able

to force that particular person to work at a much lower wage than he otherwise would, and leave him without the protection of the international brotherhood of electrical workers to stand up and speak for him. I hope the minister will bring this matter to the attention of his officials in his department because it is not a good situation.
The future of the distant early warning line, which employs many hundreds of Canadians, is a tenuous one, and there will be further retrenchments until finally the line will be of no more use at all. Indeed there are those who argue that it is already obsolete. The problem will be a recurring one, so perhaps the officials can do something now.
I hope the minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will make it clear in no uncertain terms to the government of the United States, which after all is the contractor in this matter-it is the D.E.W. line of the United States air force-that we are not prepared to accept the proposition that United States citizens should get substantially higher wages than Canadians for identical positions. If these two ministers would do this, that in itself might effect a change.
In the few minutes left to me there are a couple of other brief matters I want to mention to the minister. At one stage in the game I asked the minister whether his department would consider establishing a national employment service office in the Northwest Territories. All we want is one office in the whole of the territories. People looking for work anywhere in the far north must at the present time register with the Edmonton office, if they are in the west, or with the Montreal office if they come from the eastern part of the territories. Similarly I hope the national unemployment insurance commission will establish an office. The answer I got from the minister, as reported at page 1450 of Hansard, is that his officials have the matter under constant survey. This is surely civil service jargon for saying: We don't intend to do anything; in fact, we are not even sure where Yellowknife is. That might have been written in between the lines of the minister's answer.
I would suggest to the minister that we had an excellent example of this shortly after that. As a result of a fire in a mine at Yellowknife, at the Consolidated mine, or the "Con" mine, some 150 men had to be laid off while extensive repairs were made. Not only did these men have to apply to Edmonton,

some 600 miles further south, to register for work or for unemployment insurance benefits, but when they made application they found there were no forms available. Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, the Department of Labour, in the words of the minister's answer, having this matter under constant review and assessment and they did not even have the forms available for men to apply for these benefits? Therefore I hope the Minister of Labour will review the matter again. The number of people unemployed or who require the services of his officials is reasonably small, but I think it is important that we re-establish and reopen a national employment service office in the area. I should also like to make a comment on the winter home construction bonus of $500. The minister gave me an answer the other day which is revealing because it showed that there was only one community in the whole of the north which even applied for the bonus, and that was the community of Hay River. I do not know when winter comes and goes in Inverness-Richmond, but I do know that we in the Northwest Territories have been wintering for months by the time his official winter arrives.
I would suggest to him that the program would have real merit if he were to offer the bonus for summer home construction. I think the program might have the benefit that he claims for it in southern Canada if he carried the scheme on in the north in the summer. I would also suggest to him that while he is doing these things and his officials are looking into the need for labour legislation and how they can give leadership to the territorial

council, and while they are studying ways in which Federal Electric Corporation is discriminating against Canadian employees on the line, he also ask for a special study by his department as to what they might do to make the municipal winter works program and the house construction program more effective in the Canadian north. I would conclude at this point, Mr. Chairman, with the repetition of a statement I made to the minister of northern affairs on Friday, when I asked him to do something else. Mr. Chairman, we on this side of the house would like to know what steps the government and the Minister of Labour intend to take to solve unemployment now prevailing in Canada. During the last election campaign the candidates of the Liberal party stated that they had found solutions to settle the unemployment problem once and for all.
I see the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I remember that when we were on the government side, he delivered long speeches pointing out that he had the readymade solution to settle the unemployment problem. We would be very pleased on this side of the house if the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs gave some advice to the hon. Minister of Labour or still told us what steps this government has taken to settle the unemployment problem once and for all.
Mr. Chairman, the unemployment situation is all the more alarming as, at this time, the province of Quebec has 39 per cent of the total number of unemployed in Canada. And those who have used up their unemployment benefits or who are on unemployment as-

sistance or social welfare are not included in those statistics. According to the d.b.s., Quebec had 105,000 unemployed last June, that is the same number as in June 1962. I should like the Minister of Labour to tell us what plans the government has in mind to settle that situation.
Mr. Chairman, I do not like to mention the promises made by the Liberal candidates during the election campaigns, but their promises were quite definite in that matter and the unemployment situation gives rise to such concern that it is proper to recall them to the house. And on that matter, let me quote a letter to the editor published in Le Devoir of April 29, 1963 and entitled:
Comments by the hon. member for Montreal-St. James on the April 8 votation.
That mark of confidence will also be for me an encouragement to multiply my efforts to provide employment for the many unemployed and to alleviate the distress of certain families and certain individuals in co-operation with the civic and religious authorities.

Such a mark of confidence can only fire with enthusiasm a public man steeped in patriotism, concerned with economic prosperity and social security, so that all Canadians, whatever their ethnic origin, their language or their level of education, can realize that in this nation, they can, without any discrimination and as full partners, make a bright future for themselves and for those who will follow them.

Mr. Chairman, apart from the hon. members for Levis and Bonaventure, I also see my good friend the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) and the hon. hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay). I shall ask them to tell us why the government decided to cancel the railway construction project in the Gaspe peninsula, which would have contributed to the economic advancement and development of that district? Why?
I do not see any logical answer to this question. Moreover, the chamber of commerce of North Gaspe in a unanimous resolution, blamed the government for cancelling the railway building project in Gaspe; this resolution, which was rather hard for this government, was moved, among others, by Mr. Jourdain, former Liberal member for that district in the Quebec legislature.
This government cancelled the project, which would have largely contributed to the economic revival of Canada, but, on the other hand, it let a contract for building three submarines to the United Kingdom, at a cost of $30 million. Why deprive that part of the province of Quebec-Gaspe-of the money required for its economic development?
We would be very pleased if the Minister of Industry and Defence Production would tell us whether he proposes to grant to the French companies Peugeot and Renault, car manufacturers, the same tariff concessions he has granted the Swedish company Volvo, so that those two companies may open up plants in the province of Quebec?
I am in favour of selling wheat to foreign countries, but I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) not to make such sales at the expense of the textile industries in eastern Ontario, the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces.
We are in favour of wheat exports to foreign countries; they help to counteract our unfa-

vourable trade balance. On the other hand, I would not want such exports to be made at the expense of the textile industries in eastern Canada.

Canada will import from China products amounting to $7 million.

In rising to take part in this debate, I want to criticize the government, the Minister of Industry, the Minister of Labour and those who share responsibility for selecting the designated areas on a six months basis, using the summer months instead of the whole year. I noticed that in the announcement it was claimed the criteria for the selection of the areas had been based on the employment and unemployment figures for the summer months, rather than an average. This avoided undue emphasis on winter unemployment in areas where the problem is definitely seasonal in character.
I should like to point out that by selecting some of the areas that were chosen, the government has definitely selected areas where unemployment is seasonal in character. In this regard, I refer to the selection of Windsor and Brantford which were very poor choices. The unemployment in these areas is seasonal in nature because during the summer months, for example, the auto industry is retooling, as is the farm machinery industry. These two areas enjoy steady employment during the winter months. I feel that this type of legislation is detrimental to our way of life. So far as I know, there was no consultation with the municipalities that were designated, and

some of these areas were designated against their wishes.
The government has now promised a reappraisal of these areas within a month. However he and his government have seen fit to retain the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery, even when they see it is harming our industries and raising costs so high the companies find it extremely difficult to compete with foreign manufacturers in the Canadian market.
The imbalance of trade between tb j United States and Canada is increasing, tc Canada's disadvantage. This government is wiping out the advantages a Conservative government gave this country when they were in power. Here is something that is very interesting. Now, with the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery, this government is taxing manufacturers between $1,300 and $1,500 to create work for a man.

I should like to warn the government that the trade balance between Canada and the United States is not healthy today.

Mr. Chairman, what I have to say tonight will not be of a particularly critical nature. In fact I hope it will be considered as a constructive contribution. First I would like to thank the Minister of Labour for the occasions that he has been receptive to me in his office, and to give him credit for the manner in which I am sure he is trying to conduct his duties. I would be remiss if I did not also pay tribute to the former minister of labour as I am sure almost every
