I should like to deal with the employer incentive that was offered last winter to encourage the employment of people over 45 years of age. I do not know what has been the end result of it and I would be interested in finding out exactly how many people took advantage of it and were put to work. I did put a question on the order paper in this respect but the answer I received was not exactly what I thought to be right.
I wish to say a few words about the $500 bonus offered to people who built houses during the winter. I think this did something to spur a certain amount of building, but when you talk to the people who did build homes during the winter you find that they tell you they paid possibly $1,500 to $2,000 for the privilege of receiving that bonus. They paid that amount in these ways. First they paid it out in extra interest on the mortgages they contracted for their building projects. Second, they paid it out on the increased costs of building during wintertime, and third in the extra sales tax imposed upon building materials. These are things which we should consider seriously, and as a result of that program since wintertime the number of building starts has gone down. We should consider whether this plan should be pursued again next winter and I personally doubt very much that the end result of it shows very much in favour of the present administration.
We must remember that the present administration came into office on a rising economy, at a time when things were particularly good. In fact this afternoon one hon. member pointed out that the Prime Minister himself, in the course of an address in May last, admitted there had been two years of upswing in business prior to his administration taking office. On the basis of that I think we should give credit to the Minister of Labour for his decision to go along with the plans, policies and routines laid out by the former minister. That was a very wise decision on his part.
I should now like to comment on the widespread abuses of the unemployment insurance fund and to make one or two suggestions. It is my contention that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be rewritten. The act has so many loopholes which so many people take advantage of that nothing less than a rewriting of it is needed. For instance let us consider the case where both husband and wife are working. Perhaps the wife does not
Interim Supply
need the job but she is supplementing the income of the breadwinner of the family. In many instances she may only work long enough to qualify for unemployment insurance credits. I do not say this is the case with the majority of people, but many are taking advantage of this loophole in the act.
I believe the family should be considered as a unit and the credits or benefits accumulated by both the husband and wife should be accumulated in the name of the head of the family. Then too there is the case of a married woman working, and by reason of pregnancy she has to quit her work. Under such circumstances I do not believe she should receive unemployment insurance. If the family needs assistance there are other social agencies to provide it, and if the need is apparent they should get that assistance.
Another matter has to do with the classification of people who list themselves for employment. For example, a man who may be an architect may not be able to get a job in his own field, and if he accepts a job as a draftsman he drops in his classification. But if he does not accept employment as a draftsman he can still get his unemployment insurance. I contend such a man should be permitted to drop down in his classification and then when a job turns up in his own field he should be allowed to return to his former classification.
The same holds true for a bricklayer who cannot get a job. If he can secure employment as a hodcarrier and later transfer back to his own type of work he should be permitted to return to his former classification. Further, I suggest that we should give brooms to many people who receive unemployment insurance and send them out to sweep the sidewalks. The busy mind is a contented mind; I can myself recall taking a job in a blacksmith shop in 1929 at a time when employment was hard to find. I recall working six days of the week, 10 hours a day for 30 cents an hour, and I was glad to get the job. We did not have the type of social system then that we have today. I do not say this is to be deplored. On the contrary, such things are wonderful; but they should not be abused. Back in those days when things were tough, we did not miss any meals: However, Mr. Chairman we postponed them sometimes for an indefinite period.
I think the majority of our people really and truly want to work, but there are a few people who are leeches and who are taking advantage of the loopholes which exist in this act. Last year, a firm of which I happen

Interim Supply
to be a director asked me if I could make a contact at the local unemployment office and try to obtain ten labourers. There were none available. However, there was a group of people hanging around and I went to see some of them. I asked them if they were interested in going to work, and the first question they asked me was: What do you pay? I told them we paid $1.75 an hour for a 40 hour week, which would give them a gross return of $70. I recall a couple of them saying to me: "Why should we work for that? We would be working for only $34, because we are getting $36 now in unemployment insurance. All you are giving us is a little better than 75 cents an hour." The result was they just did not agree to take the work which was offered them and eventually we had to hire other men and get along in the meantime as best we could.
I think it is time we showed a little more objectivity with regard to these things. It is time we got down to bringing legislation before this house to protect ourselves against some of these evils and to protect the unemployment insurance fund as well. In fact I believe we should revamp this entire act. I am of the opinion that we should pay a man a decent day's wages for an honest day's work. In this way I am sure we will make better citizens.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I should like to take this opportunity to say a few words on the estimates of the Department of Labour in order to bring to the attention of the minister a few of the problems with which we are confronted on the east coast and, in particular, on Cape Breton island.
I know the minister is getting back home every once in a while now, and I trust as a result he will be better informed about just what the situation is there in regard to unemployment. Hon. members have mentioned today and on other occasions the fine job the minister is doing. I will say this: The minister is always a gentleman. He is always prepared to give proper answers in the house. And how could he be anything else but a gentleman, seeing he comes from Cape Breton?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that logic?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Frankly, I think the minister may be too much of a gentleman in certain places-and here I refer to the treasury board and the cabinet room. I would think that, being such a nice fellow, the bookkeeper from Toronto is encouraged at times to get out his knife and

cut and slash government expenditures on the east coast. I do wish that at times the minister would forget he is such a gentleman, and get a little rough once in a while, in treasury board and in cabinet meetings. He should start banging a few tables and letting them know that he is from Cape Breton, and that the people in that area would like some attention. We need to have a strong minister from Nova Scotia to look after our interests both in treasury board and in cabinet as well. One is confronted there by men like the Minister of Industry who, I presume, would not consider 100 jobs very much since he comes from a large metropolitan area where enterprises of this size are common. But on Cape Breton island, in Nova Scotia and in the Atlantic provinces generally, this represents a lot of employment and it means a lot to those who get it.
I should like to use as a text this evening several extracts from a speech prepared for delivery by the Minister of Labour to the trade union summer school at St. Francis Xavier University at Antigonish, Nova Scotia on June 24, 1964. He said:
I am very glad to be back again at St. Francis Xavier to catch at least a fleeting glimpse of your trade union summer school in action and to say a few words to you. I had the great honour of coming back here just over a month ago to accept an honorary degree and address the graduating class.
A little belatedly I should like to extend to my good friend-I think, and hope he is-and colleague from Cape Breton, whose riding adjoins my own, hearty congratulations on receiving this honorary degree from his old university.
The minister went on to say:
One of my staff has suggested that if I'm going to keep coming back like this, giving lectures as I used to do for a living, I'm in danger of being accused of moonlighting.
I do not know if he would be accused of moonlighting too much, but certainly he can be accused of giving lectures, because almost daily the minister gives lectures in different parts of the country. He says a lot of nice things, and when he goes east he has a lot of nice things to say; but we want some action from the minister in regard to his policies or plans for those who are unemployed in Canada, including the Atlantic coast, of course. He went on to say:
I can assure you that for a long time to come my cabinet colleagues and I won't have any time for moonlighting unless your panel on "organizing the unorganized" have already laid plans for organizing cabinet ministers and are prepared to go for a 70 hour week for us.

I know the minister is quite modest, and I wonder if he is suggesting that he is working 70 hours. Maybe so. However, I would hope that in this long stint he is putting in he has given some time and concentration to the question of what is going to be done for those who are continually being laid off from work, fired, released, or whatever you want to call it, at the Point Edward naval base as a result of his colleague's action and announcement-here I refer to the Minister of National Defence-of December 5 last, when he decided he would close the Point Edward naval base. 1 wonder whether in that hard work he is doing he is thinking very actively of raising strong objections now to the cabinet and his colleagues, as the minister from Nova Scotia, against these lay-offs and is pointing out the hardship involved, fighting within the cabinet for these people, in order to find them alternative employment.
I have here a newspaper item which appeared in the Cape Breton Post of February 5, 1964. It is headed, "350 involved". I have reason to believe this figure will be slightly over 400 before the government is through retiring these workers who have been employed at the base. The article says:
Relocation is promised.
Commander E. B. Morris, superintendent of the Point Edward naval base, said Tuesday that plans are being completed for the relocation of approximately 350 civilian personnel at the ship repair facility for alternative employment.
The closure of the ship repair facility was first announced by defence minister Hellyer on December 5 as part of the department's cut-back in defence expenditures.
"The Department of National Defence, in conjunction with the Department of Labour, has been investigating alternative job opportunities for civilian personnel affected by the closing of the ship repair facility", he said in a statement.
That was back in early February of this year. I am wondering how many of the employees who were laid off at the naval base have been re-employed or relocated through the offices of the Minister of Labour. It has been my duty and privilege to write to the minister on quite a number of occasions with regard to constituents who have been thrown out of employment by this government. The minister very courteously replies to me and tells me he is going to get the national employment service to do whatever they can to assist these people. Unfortunately, on many occasions I have further and repetitive letters from these same people as time goes by, saying they have not received the employment that was promised.
Interim Supply
I would like to ask the minister what is going to be done for these people who have been laid off, and are being laid off, at the naval base. Did the minister protest very vehemently in cabinet against the closure of this base? I think in an area such as we have on the east coast the base should have been kept open, because despite all the slashing the Minister of National Defence has done, surely there must still be the odd schooner or something to be repaired in the navy. I do not know just what he has left. It is not too much; but whatever is left to be repaired for the navy could easily be carried out at the Point Edward naval base. The work was performed there, and it was excellent. I do not ask the minister to accept that statement just because I say it, but naval authorities have advised me that the work performed at the base was as good as that performed anywhere in Canada. So surely that is not the reason for the closure of this base.
For some time now we have had discussions in Cape Breton in regard to the opening of a new coal mine. I am sure the minister is very familiar with the discussions that have been going on at these meetings of civic authorities, union authorities and others concerned. I would hope he would use his position as Minister of Labour to encourage these discussions to continue, with the object of the Dominion Coal Company starting a new opening in Cape Breton. I would also hope that no restrictions have been placed on the Dominion Coal Company by the government in regard to the amount of money they would receive in the way of subventions in relation to shipments of coal, we will say to Ontario hydro. I would hope the minister would have an opportunity to reply to this question and state very definitely that no limitations have been put on this coal company in the event that they do produce more coal than is being produced at the present time. I also hope he will encourage the opening of this mine. Mr. J. E. Clubb, president of Dominion Coal Company, said recently in an interview, when discussing the possibility of opening a new coal mine, that because of the federal government's subventions-treasury assistance to get coal to market-the government would have to concur before money could be spent to open the Lingan seam in Cape Breton. So Mr. Clubb is saying in so many words that if the government will give him authorization in this regard and say, "Look, fellows; you go ahead and start your coal mine, and if you can find markets in Ontario we will provide the subventions necessary to ship

Interim Supply
that coal to market", his company can go ahead. At the present time it is my understanding that 15 per cent of the coal that is consumed by Ontario hydro is Canadian and 85 per cent is American. I would hope the minister would be able to point out to his colleagues in the cabinet that this 15 per cent consumed by Ontario hydro should be increased to at least 25 per cent and that the necessary subventions should be forthcoming from the dominion treasury.
Some hon. members opposite from Ontario may perhaps be saying to themselves: We have to send these poormouth people in the Atlantic provinces some more money. Certainly industries in central Canada are protected. I am thinking of the automobile industry, the manufacturers of refrigerators and washing machines, or "white goods" as they are known in the trade, also television sets and that sort of thing which are protected by tariffs. Would it not be better to provide subventions to transport coal and keep people working in Cape Breton rather than have them on unemployment insurance? I think it would be a much better suggestion, and I plead with the minister to forget that he is such a nice fellow and to get before treasury board on the matter, because I am sure he could really stir his colleagues up if he put his heart into it.
As a result of the closing of the naval base and the cutting off of minesweepers on the east coast by the Minister of National Defence

I am sure many people in Cape Breton just love him because of his action in this regard-we find that the private yards in Cape Breton island are not receiving any work. They handled a lot of the minesweepers and other smaller craft. Most of the work was done at the naval base but part of it was done at private yards. Last week when the minister went home he met a union representative there with regard to the North Sydney Marine Railway Company, Limited. They used to be quite busy. In fact, when we were in government they received more allocations of naval ships at that yard than in any other comparable period. Now, strangely enough, since this government has come into power they find they are not receiving refits, and as a result their employees have no work to do.
In the July 25 issue of the Cape Breton Post there is a report which says that the Minister of Labour stated he would do everything possible to keep Sydney Engineering and Drydock operating at capacity. This

is another private yard in Cape Breton. The report goes on:
Dry dock employees, members of the industrial union of marine workers and shipbuilders of Canada, said Thursday the staff of Sydney Engineering and Drydock has been reduced by 50 per cent because of the loss of contracts from the Point Edward naval base.
Mr. MaeEachen, who arrived in Sydney yesterday on a brief visit to his home constituency of Inverness-Richmond, said government officials are aware of the problem at the drydock here.
"We have discussed this problem with company officials and the government is doing everything possible to remedy the situation," Mr. MaeEachen said.
They are very nice words, but that statement does not put people to work. If no naval refits are allocated to this yard surely this government of so-called action-I do not say "action" because it is really so-called; the government have not shown very much action except retreating from budgets, and that sort of thing-can find alternative employment for these people who are being laid off at the private yards.
A few months ago the Minister of Transport addressed a board of trade meeting in North Sydney, and the March 16 issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald carries the heading "Poor-house attitude must go, Pickersgill". The report continues:
The Atlantic region had to rid itself of the "poorhouse" attitude, transport minister J. W. Pickersgill said here Saturday.
It was not enough for the Atlantic provinces to export its products and brains. "We should get people here to see what they can attain and what they are missing."
Then the July 25 issue of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald carries the heading "Pickersgill Optimistic of Cape Breton Outlook". Then there is the following heading in today's newspaper, "Future Bright, MaeEachen Agrees with Pickersgill". The report goes on:
He said: "I agree with my colleague Mr. Pickersgill, who said Friday in Sydney that the outlook for the island is very promising."
In tomorrow's paper we will probably see another heading:	"Everything Wonderful,
Pickersgill Agrees with MaeEachen". And so we can go on scratching backs, back and forth between the two ministers, but this does not put people to work. I hope their efforts will be a little more evident than this.
I have been trying for quite a long time to find out from the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Labour-and I see the President of the Privy Council the former minister of transport looking at me and I think he knows what I am about to say- what is going to happen to the employees

at the C.N.R. docks in North Sydney, when and if this proposed new ferry is constructed. According to the Minister of Transport this ferry is going to carry loaded railway freight cars from the port of North Sydney to Port aux Basques. There will be no handling at the port of North Sydney. Both ministers have continually in their replies and letters to the stevedores union at North Sydney, local 1259 I.L.A., said that freight will increase every year; that it always increases every year. It is true, it does increase on average about 4 or 5 per cent per year. That is good; we like it and hope it continues. But if the government are going to put in service a ship which will take loaded railway cars aboard, there will not be any handling at all at North Sydney. As a result I suggest that employment will be curtailed at least 75 per cent.
This belief is supported by the secretary of the union and the others concerned. I beg and plead with the minister, please, to answer whether or not a railway freight car ferry is going to be put into operation. Again I ask him to forget that he is such a nice chap and to go to cabinet and get before treasury board and change this, because it will drastically injure the economy of the town of North Sydney, Sydney Mines and the surrounding areas. Would he also clarify the situation for the benefit of the port commission in North Sydney, the mayor of North Sydney, the mayor of Sydney Mines who is a very dear friend of the Minister of Labour, and particularly and most importantly the men who are presently employed at these places who are looking forward to continuing employment. However, if this sort of thing goes into effect we will again see the lay-offs which are occurring at the Point Edward naval base.
I do not know how else to put my case. I have tried to ask the minister in as plain language as possible. Unfortunately I am not bilingual or I would put it to him in French. I know only a few words of Gaelic, and I am sure that he knows more than I, so I cannot go far there. However, I ask him in plain, simple, everyday language to rise to his feet and to tell us that the government is not going to put this type of ferry into operation, but that the status quo will remain and we will have the normal type of vessel which is now operating. If so, I am sure that not only will I be very happy but all of those concerned will be more than happy to know that they need have no fear of the future. I shall not delay the committee any longer, other than to say that I have read the speech
Interim Supply
that was delivered for the minister, I understand, because he could not be there, and I found it quite interesting. I hope he will now try to bring about some of the things he suggested in his speech. At one point he said:
Some radio programs are criticized because the audience is told what it is going to hear.. .and then it is told what it has heard. Tonight I'm going to change that a bit by first telling you what you are not going to hear.
He goes on to tell them what they are not going to hear and then says:
Finally, you are not going to hear a catalogue in detail of those things the government and my department in particular are doing in the pursuit of an active manpower policy for Canada and the realization of full employment.
As a result of some of the things that have happened in Cape Breton in the last year we will never reach what he terms full employment. He goes on to say:
I may touch on some of these things from time to time as necessary but I shall not go into detail about subjects on which I am sure you are already informed. Instead I am going to talk about poverty.
Goodness knows, if he and the government continue in the manner in which they have we are going to have a lot of poverty, and no one knows better than the minister the serious situation in eastern Canada, Cape Breton island and particularly his own riding of Inverness-Richmond.
The time has come, Mr. Chairman, not for a nice, gentlemanly cabinet minister from Nova Scotia, although that is a good asset, but one who will be active and who will tell his colleagues sitting beside him, the Secretary of State and the Minister of National Defence, about the seriousness of things on the east coast. He might also look to his left and suggest to the Solicitor General that he too might do something about some of the serious problems in Prince Edward Island. I am sure the Solicitor General knows of the seriousness of the situation there. I can see his alertness now.
The time has come for a man who will stand up to treasury board and in cabinet and tell treasury board, the members of the cabinet and the Prime Minister of the country, who wandered up and down throughout the country making all kinds of extravagant promises about the government he was going to create, that prompt action is needed. Actually people on the east coast are getting sick and tired and fed up with the pious platitudes that have been thrown at them by the Minister of Transport, and now the Minister of Labour is guilty of the same thing. This

Interim Supply
shocks me because I would expect it from the Minister of Transport but not from the Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Why not?

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Probably he has the same speech writer or the same person issuing news releases. In any event, what is the minister going to do to provide alternative employment for those who have been thrown on the street by the government at Point Edward naval base? What is the Minister of Labour going to do for those who have been thrown out of employment at private yards which are not receiving any naval refits? As the representative in the cabinet from Nova Scotia, what is the minister going to do in regard to getting a new coal mine started in Cape Breton? Is he going to get the assurance that whatever subventions are necessary will be forthcoming from the government to enable coal to be shipped to Ontario? What is the minister going to do with regard to the proposed ferry for North Sydney, having regard to the way the Minister of Transport has dealt with this matter? The Minister of Transport made a wonderful announcement about a new ferry at a board of trade meeting in North Sydney but he did not tell the 200 people assembled there what type of ferry it would be. We all stood up and applauded him. This was a terrific thing because it would provide employment. Then he went over in the corner with the representatives of the Cape Breton Post and the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, and whispered in their ears that it would be a railway freight car ferry. The board of trade meeting was on Saturday night and the Minister of Transport was safe and sound in Newfoundland when the newspapers came out on Monday. I cannot understand why he did not say this to all those assembled at the board of trade meeting. I sat right next to the minister and we had a lovely meal, but his speech was not very good. It was all right as far as he went but why did he not tell the whole story? Then we could have approached him right there. Now we are trying daily and weekly in this house to find out something about it.
I trust that my very good friend and colleague, the Minister of Labour, has listened rather attentively to the three or four points I have made. I am sure I can look forward to his rising in his place and allaying all fears in regard to the ferry, telling us that there is going to be employment for the men who have been laid off at Point Edward and at the

private yards, and putting our minds at rest with regard to the other things I have mentioned, particularly the new coal mine.

Mr. Chairman, I know there is some sort of agreement to keep silent on the part of the splinter parties, which apparently are no longer part of the opposition. They are going to remain silent. I do not know what has prompted this but I throw out a challenge to them. They are the planners. They are even greater planners than the Liberal party. They claim to be. But when there is a need for planning what do they do? They remain silent. They appear to me to be a group of overpaid and overrated gossips. Hon. members know whom I mean. I think $18,000 a year is a lot of money to pay people to come down here to gossip over the back fence, and spend a great deal more of their time criticizing their colleagues than they do in giving leadership to the government.
I do not think our party fits into this group. We are in a constructive mood. Ever since this session began we have, without change of plan or tactics, continually offered to the government constructive criticism on every piece of poor legislation they have brought in, which just about covers the waterfront. Since we came here for this session we have not had one piece of legislation that was fit to be O.K'd by us. We are being paid enough now to use what brains we have, even if they are limited, so let us use them and stop the bickering and the gossiping and get on with the job.
For fear of being accused of being one of this group myself, may I say that since I first came to the house I have never risen to my feet without offering as much constructive advice as I have been able to muster, and some kind of solution. Whether I am right or wrong I think that is the proper attitude and I have had enough gossip for tonight.
Today we are dealing with labour matters, Mr. Chairman, and I do not think you will have to remind me to stay on labour matters because what I wish to say now is strictly within the ambit of the Department of Labour. We have got into a lot of trouble because there has not been planning. I will not blame the Mackenzie King government, the Bennett government, the St. Laurent government or the Diefenbaker government. I will not say they have been guilty of not planning, but to a certain extent the planning has not been done. Our excuse has often been that we do not believe in regimentation. No,

we do not; but you can have planning without regimentation. You can also have useless planning, which is away off the mark and wastes itself like a stream in the desert. But we can have constructive planning, and if we had had constructive planning over a period of years in the Department of Labour I would venture to say we would not be in the jam we are today with the labour people. I take Mr. Banks as a glowing example of what happens when the labour department of Canada abdicates its responsibility.
We need a labour code for Canada. The lawyers in the house will get up and say this is unconstitutional; you are interfering with provincial rights. I do not know of anything upon which we can legislate which does not affect the provinces. We can legislate on labour in the dominion. Now we are going to have labouring people who want to grasp the bull by the horns, so we are going to have labour unions in the civil service. Who is going to be helped if we do have the kind of unions we have in the service. You will have a labour union for the mounted police, a labour union for your nurses, and yet labour won't have the right to run its own affairs.
You will never have the right to work if labour unions are run by gangsters. You will never keep the gangsters out so long as they have their machine guns in the back rooms, or the economic machine guns. Which is worse, to point a machine gun loaded with bullets at me or to face me with unemployment and starvation for my family? I am not afraid of bullets in machine guns, but there have been times when I have been afraid of unemployment. You are not going to get rid of the labour bosses or find a solution for the problem talking in parliament. What is the solution? Just give the little people of Canada the right to choose their own leaders the same as we have the right to choose our leaders in parliament. We do not always choose well, but nevertheless the right is there. I claim that if you give the working man of Canada the right to choose his own leaders he would not choose men like Banks and those other fellows. In the United States if the working men had that right they would not have men like Hoffa running their affairs. Give the union members a secret ballot, the same kind of ballot you have yourself for election to the House of Commons. Give this to the labouring man of Canada. If you do not do that, all the rest of the talk we have about labour here is quite useless. If a man cannot
Interim Supply
go behind the curtain and say he does not like Mr. Banks, then you will have Mr. Banks, Mr. McLaughlin or some other goon brought in here. If you cannot raise that type of gangster here in Canada, then he will be imported from the United States, with the so-called help of the departments of government that do not do their job for the little people of Canada.
I do not believe we need labour unions at all, if we do our job in this House of Commons. We need to establish minimum wages. This is a hundred years overdue. There should not be anybody working in Canada who does not take home enough money to buy socks and shoes and so on for the children. Perhaps if we did that, we would not need this social legislation they rant about down in the corner. But I notice they want their $18,000 a year. Oh, I know the old gossip gets out, and apparently in his column he says we are obstructing. He is obstructing nothing. We are only doing the things which these planners should be doing themselves. If there is any virtue in socialism, it is in planning. What are their plans? Here is one; but would they vote for a labour code to give the right to the labouring people to run their own affairs? They would not.
If you give the secret ballot to the people in the labour movement, they would clean up their own unions. We would not need any maritime board of trustees or anything else. These people could run their own affairs. The people of Canada have lots of guts and they would clean up their own affairs. However, this cannot be done if they have economic machine guns behind the curtain; you know what I mean. You do what you are told or you will starve to death. You need the secret ballot. Why do we need it? We need it because we are not all Christian gentlemen, you know. This is still a jungle and the labour bosses are the biggest apes in the jungle. The only way we can control these apes in parliament is by the secret ballot. If you do not do your work, the people have the right to kick you out every five years.
I have five points in my labour code. The first, and most important one, is a secret ballot. If you put in the right officers, they will put in the right bylaws. If you do not have the secret ballot, you will not have the right officers and you will not have a properly conducted labour union. I am not in favour of the control of labour unions. If you have the secret ballot, who is going to elect a United States goon to run a labour union in

Interim Supply
Canada? The United States goons are in competition with us. Why, when John L. Lewis, calls out his miners in Alberta, that benefits the miners in Pennsylvania? There are ten miners in Pennslyvania in the union to every one in Alberta, so how are you going to get a square deal in Canada? There is no point in running to the government and asking the government to kick them out. We cannot kick them out. Only one man can kick them out and that is the working man who goes behind the curtain to mark his X, in secret.
If you do not have United States bosses, you will not have to pay dues to the United States. You will not have to pay John L. Lewis to run our unions. He would not do anything for you if he could not come in here and collect his dues. Where are these fellows in the splinter parties? Do they stand up for a code like this? They are afraid, and I will tell you why. They hurl insults across the floor at the Liberals and Conservatives because they say we take dirty money from management. Where do they get their money? They get it from the controlled unions. They get it from the big bosses of labour who bring in the apes who do the physical violence such as no manufacturer ever thought of doing.
No wonder the R.C.M.P. are in bad shape.

You are lucky you have the R.C.M.P. to protect you because if you said the things you do in some countries you would be where you belong. We should control the criminal elements in a union. How do we do it, then? I think it is quite simple-1 and do not throw this provincial jurisdiction question at me. We can do this. The dominion government just arranges that it will not sign a collective bargaining agreement with any official who has had a criminal record during the last five years. I believe in rehabilitation. I believe you can live down your crimes if you live long enough. We should put these labour bosses with criminal records out of business for five years at least. Do not sign or let labour officials sign a document with a man who has been convicted of certain crimes within the last five years. Well, I will start with sedition, violence upon the person, organized murder, conspiracy to maim; these are just a few that come to my mind.
Perhaps it is my suspicious police training. I think some of it was not suspicious.
I can tell you, however, that I know what happens when they call in the R.C.M.P. to put down a strike caused by the sloppiness

of a government or the inadequacy of our own labour laws. The mounted police were never designed for this job. They were designed to keep law and order amongst people who had reasonable ethics, a reasonable chance of earning their own living. We were never intended to be strike breakers; we were never recruited as troops. I am sorry I have never said these things before. I saw the R.C.M.P. used as strike breakers in Newfoundland while the government decided to wait. The R.C.M.P. are not strike breakers, and they should not be used for that purpose. Had I been a labour man I would have wanted to be a union man because it is the only way to protect your rights, when we do not do our job in parliament.
The next point in my labour code is the right to work. It is perhaps even more important than many of the other rights which we see piously put up and written into codes. You should have the right to earn a living for your family. You cannot do this if the labour bosses call strikes, legal strikes so-called or otherwise. The working man is then forced to go out on strike and the pay cheque is taken away. We should let him have another secret ballot to decide whether or not he should continue on the job. I venture to say that we should give him a chance to go home and talk the matter over with his wife, because she wants the bread and butter for her children even if he does not care.
Give this man the secret ballot before you can have what you call a legal strike, if there is such a thing. Now, I will change the tune a little bit and go to something a little bit nicer. We will talk about our children. We get sentimental when we talk about our children. We give them the opportunity to borrow up to $5,000 at 6 per cent. We make loans to farmers at 5 per cent. I do not know whether it is more important to educate children by loans at this rate of interest, especially when they have no means of income, or to lend $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 to farmers at 5 per cent. I am not at all against lending money to farmers because this is one thing upon which I agree with the Social Crediters, that the wealth of the country should underwrite its mortgage, if that can be done.
Lending students money at 6 per cent through chartered banks is no gift. If they graduate perhaps they might be in a position to pay it back, but if they do not graduate, and are trained in a semi-academic field, it may be impossible for them to pay it back. I promised to give the answer to this situation and I shall. It is very simple, namely to

create job opportunities for young people the same as we had in good times when I was a boy. We were able to go out and work and save enough money to put ourselves through college or take a course in a technical school. We should find work for them and let them pay their own way.
I believe in a boy doing it on his own, and that is why I am a Conservative. I am not waiting for anybody to regiment me, to push me on to a campus. Give me an opportunity for a job, guarantee me a man's wages, let me work under bosses of my choice and I will save my own money to put myself through college. There were Liberals in this country who believed in that too. At one time there were only two branches of government, the ins and the outs. When the Grits came in they acted like men, and when the Conservatives came in they too expected a man to stand on his own feet; but what we have now is everybody whining for some sort of socialism. They have it in Sweden; but have they "got it made" in Sweden? Go and see the effect of it. There is no more marriage in Sweden. If you like it that way, all right. If you want it that way in Canada,
0.	K. Bring in your socialism; pull down the barriers.
This is something which has shown up in our art. Go and look in the national gallery. Nobody has the guts to stand up and say, "It's a mess,"-except for a nine year old school boy who did just that the other day. He is a quiz kid, and in my opinion he does not need any more education because he has common sense. He is a boy who has an
1.	Q. of 160, and when he was in the gallery they asked him, "What do you think of that painting over there?" He said "Where". They said "That thing over there." He said, "Oh that. You want my honest opinion or a diplomatic corps answer"? They said, "We want your honest opinion." He said, "It's a mess."
I do not know how many thousands of dollars we have paid for such things. That building over there is half full of them. We have paid out thousands of dollars for such things; as a matter of fact I think it has run into hundreds of thousands of dollars, because apparently there is nobody in this chamber with the guts to stand up like that small boy and say, "That, sir, is a mess."
We are talking about education. Where is our education going if you cannot train 265 out of 18 million people so that they will be able to walk around the national gallery and say, "Those are messes and we will not buy any more of them?" If we send kids to the
Interim Supply
Banff school of art we want them to come up with something that is recognizable by somebody. How many millions of dollars have we given to the Canada Council, and how many millions of dollars have been channelled into these programs?
I am not putting on an act. I am telling you something each one of you in your heart and guts knows is true. The people of Canada are fed up with this. They are fed up paying us $18,000 a year for sitting around here just gossiping with one another instead of getting on with the business of the country. I am not at all sure I want the election you are always throwing at us, as I may walk out of this anyway. I was earning an honest living when I came down here, but I look around and sometimes wonder how many of us can stand and say that is what we are doing now.
If you want to clean up the labour situation, give them a labour code and stand behind it. If you want Hal Banks, give me leave of absence and I will bring him in here by the ears. He may be as big as the hon. member for Port Arthur-I don't know-but if so I will get some of my pals and I will skate him in. But if you are not going to prosecute him when you bring him back, let him stay in Maine, because we have still some vestige of Canadian justice. I still believe in British justice and I am not ashamed to say that. It has given every citizen in this country a square deal, a place in the sun. Don't get rid of it, boys, any of you, because I do not know what would rush in to fill the vacuum.
Look at Africa. They got rid of the old British rule there, but would any of you move to Africa? If you would, how many of you would take your families there? How many of you want to live there? There are many places in Africa and throughout the world which would be glad to have British rule back.
What are we going to do for our children? Well, I told you-give them an opportunity to earn their own living. Stop babying them around. When 1 was 18 years of age my father said to me, "You're getting too big for your boots." "No," I said, "I am not getting too big for my boots. I bought them and I fill them." I have tried to fill them ever since. If you think you can take an 18-year-old boy and put him back with his mother, you are wrong. You might keep him alive for a few years, but you would never make a man out of him. Put him to work. Give him a chance, and my guess is he will make out. We are still Canadians.

Interim Supply
I say this to those who are sitting on the treasury benches over there: I challenge you: You lead. You said we were no good; you got us out. The Prime Minister made it. Now is the time to make it good. Do not look for help from members in that corner to my far left. They are only there because they are afraid to face the electorate. Do not have a Mussolini in your belly. You know what happened to Hitler-and I am not comparing you with Hitler. He had a weak partner. Go it alone, if you want to lead this country. If you have confidence in your ability, try to lead. Never mind this threat about an election. Never mind what happened about the Easter recess. I didn't get an Easter recess, and it was your fault. If we do not get a summer recess it won't bother me too much. We have a bigger job to do than row a boat somewhere. Let us earn our $18,000 a year. I am just getting mad enough, now, that I am going to start doing it.

My hon. friend who has just spoken has asked this government for action. Certainly, all members of this committee are hopeful that the government will produce the type of action which will be of benefit to the nation as a whole.
Mr. Lloyd George has been given credit for a statement which I recommend to the government as having some merit. He once said of a French premier that he was a man who mistook movement for action. As far as I can see, especially as far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, this has been the case. We have seen a great deal of movement, and a great many moving speeches have been made, but little that is constructive or helpful has been accomplished to date. Indeed, I find that today, 15 months after this government assumed office, the maritime provinces are in the position of not knowing what their future is likely to be. They do not know where they are, under this government, and they do not know what they can look forward to.
I am sure we are entitled to know what our future prospects are and what role our people are to play. Only recently we read in the Halifax newspaper that the Minister of Agriculture had agreed with a report which stated that we should take half the people in Nova Scotia off their farms and put them to work in a more constructive way. This appears to me to be the type of philosophy expounded by the present Minister of Finance when he was an oracle preaching the gospel for the Liberal party. This might be quite true. If it is, then I ask: What is this

government doing about it? What does it intend to do about it? My reference has been to agriculture, but it is certainly related to employment.
Let us consider the position of the Minister of Industry, bearing in mind that he is also Minister of Defence Production, and ask him the same question from the point of view of the Atlantic provinces. The problem which arises each day the present government remains in office is that one minister says one thing and another minister says another. There is no co-ordination within the cabinet, no clear voice which indicates to us what our future is likely to be and what role this government intends to play to help make the days ahead better for our people than they are at the present time.
We have a minister from Nova Scotia at the head of the Department of Labour. It is true there is no better portfolio for a minister from the maritime provinces to hold, for there is one area in Canada where chronic unemployment remains the order of the day, and it is the maritime provinces. However we have heard nothing from the hon. gentleman to date about any over-all comprehensive type of program which would help us know what our future is likely to be, and what this government intends to do to make it better. In particular, we have not been told what measures are to be taken, if any, to rid us of the growing unemployment problem which remains with us year after year.
Let us compare what has been promised by the present administration with what was achieved under the former Conservative government. Under the former administration, the people of the Atlantic provinces definitely knew where they were going. They saw our government producing basic philosophies and enacting legislation which was of real benefit to them. They knew that any action taken on their part would be followed by action of merit on the part of the administration here in Ottawa. This has not been the case since the present government took office, despite the fact that no party ever offered more pie in the sky than did the present administration. We must be given an over-all picture of the policy of this government as it relates to the Atlantic area, if we are to be able to appreciate-what our future needs are likely to be and what the priorities of the provincial governments should be as far as their spending programs are concerned. They should mesh together. There should be no fear that provincial and federal governments are going in different directions. We should be certain.

that our people are utilizing the assets they have in the best possible manner.
In confirmation of what I am saying, I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on June 10 of this year relating to a statement made by Dr. Harry Johnson, a professor who formerly taught the present Minister of Labour. Among other things, Dr. Johnson had this to say; he said unemployment in Canada had been relieved not by good policies but by good luck. Well, we have not been as fortunate in the maritime provinces as have some other areas of Canada and we have not had the same degree of good luck as has been experienced by some areas in this country. Oh, it is always good to look at statistics in July and August and say: "Things are not so bad in the Atlantic provinces because the figure for unemployment there is only 4 per cent or 5 per cent." There is always plenty of employment in the Atlantic provinces in the summertime. But every winter, without fail, the unemployment figures run two to three times as great there as in other parts of Canada. This is not a situation which can be altered by prayers. You do it by action, and you do not accomplish it by movement alone; there has to be action associated with that movement before there can be any assurance that the future will be better than the past. And no decisions of this kind have been forthcoming from the present government since it took office.
As some further evidence of the point of view of the people of the Atlantic provinces and particularly of Nova Scotia on this subject, I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Tuesday, July 21. The editor was discussing the situation which confronts the Minister of Industry in his capacity as such and also in his capacity as Minister of Defence Production. He says:
One should expect, on the other hand, that Mr. Drury would review his defence production decisions in the light of his responsibilities as the minister in charge of area development. Thus if it is possible to let contracts of this kind in provinces or areas with lagging economies, and if, in so doing, the government involves itself in an extra expense, it should be possible to charge this differential not to defence productions, but to the accounts of the area development agency.
If this were done, Mr. Drury and his successors in the industry portfolio could discharge their responsibilities to the taxpayer on the one hand and give effect to the principle, on the other, that Ottawa has a burden to carry in the general effort to equalize, as much as is possible, economic opportunity across the country.
Interim Supply
Certainly, if some such rationalization is not worked out within the industry department soon, it is clear that the Fairey Canada episode will repeat itself many times, and that defence production-as far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned-will be a constant bone of contention.
Worse, whatever good the area development people in the department of industry may accomplish will be washed out in the public mind by a defence procurement policy which seems to negate it at every turn.
The editor of the Springfield Record writing along similar lines, had this to say:
Those who get a bit tired of Quebeckers complaining that they are being discriminated against in Canada must have been a bit shocked when they read an article by Eric Dennis in Monday's Chronicle-Herald pointing out that Quebec in recent years has been receiving one half of all government major defence contracts awarded in Canada. Of the $277,000,000 spent in Canada in the top four defence-buying-fields-ships, aircraft and parts, electronics and instruments-$144,000,000 went to Montreal firms and some $6,000,000 to other Quebec firms. Toronto and Ontario received $101,000,000 and the rest of Canada $26,000,000. In 1962-63 expenditures in Quebec amounted to $130,000,000; Ontario $93,000,000, an the rest of Canada $36,000,000.
It begins to look as though Canadians outside of Quebec should be demanding equal opportunities with Quebec. Certainly, there seems little justification in their snatching the little bit of defence business that comes to Nova Scotia.
Those are the points of view of Nova Scotians. I hope that in the not too distant future the Minister of Labour will see to it that the Atlantic provinces, and the mari-times in particular, are provided with a statement of where we can expect to go if this government remains in office; what we can expect to look forward to from the Department of Industry, from the Department of Defence Production and from the Department of Agriculture-from every department that touches on the vitality of our economy. Then we may better know whether there is any value in paying attention to the words that pour forth from those that come into our area, words which are never followed by the deeds we have been led to believe would follow.
I ask the minister to consider my constituency and to look at the situation of the town of Springhill. I ask him where that town is going; where it has gone since this government took office. What has this government done? What incidental thing has the government done to assist the unemployed in that area to any degree at all? They have done nothing whatsoever. Indeed, they have done their best to set back the economy of that hard-luck town by playing politics and by using patronage to delay the construction of an

Interim Supply
institution which will become the backbone of the town's economy if it is ever constructed. Each time I put a question on the order paper asking the government to indicate to me what action is forthcoming, I am told one thing. Then the month arrives when this action is supposed to take place; I then look for positive indications of the action that has been promised, and there are no indications whatsoever.
Here is an opportunity for a government to assist materially an area that has been bearing more than its fair share of the burdens related to unemployment. Contrary to this government doing anything to assist, and contrary to the Minister of Labour, Nova Scotia's representative in the cabinet, taking concrete steps to see that these people are assisted, we are faced with delays, either deliberate or otherwise, that only help to bring a further degree of difficulty to the people in that community-and these people do not deserve to face any further difficulty. Our minister should feel ashamed of the actions of this government in relation to that town. He should feel ashamed of his own actions in this regard and the fact he has not seen that something is done for the people there.
I hope the minister will rise before 10.30 and indicate to the committee that something will be done for the Atlantic provinces, something that is co-ordinative, constructive and geared to helping us try to equalize the opportunities in our area of Canada as compared with the rest of Canada; and to let the people of Springhill know that in the not too distant future they will have opportunities to go to work-because this is all they are asking.

Mr. Chairman, I would not like to pass up this opportunity to debate matters pertaining to the Department of Agriculture, and I am sure the Minister of Labour will not be surprised when I rise in my seat and speak on this matter. In particular I would like to deal with the Gill report. That report was presented to the government of the day in November, 1962, and it is 20 months, or almost two years, since it was presented to the House of Commons and the Minister of Labour. But the minister and the government have failed to present the report to the house so that we may debate the matters contained therein, in particular those matters pertaining to agricultural labour.
I still cannot understand why the agricultural labourer is the only working man not covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
IMr. Coates.]
It has been said on more than one occasion that it is because agricultural labourers are seasonal workers; but what about the fishing industry? They are also seasonal workers. What about the lumber industry, whose workers are also seasonal? What about the construction industry? All these industries employ seasonal workers. But when this question is raised in regard to the seasonal farm labourer, it is said that similar provisions cannot be implemented in regard to them. We read this in the Gill report:
We recommend that the general principle be followed of extending coverage as broadly as possible so long as the necessary administrative procedures may be carried out to see to it that the rules of the plan are adhered to in a satisfactory fashion.
That is referring to unemployment insurance coverage for seasonal workers in agriculture. If the seasonal fishermen, the seasonal lumber workers and all the other employees can be covered by unemployment insurance, certainly the farm labourer should be covered also. Farmers are losing money by not having the opportunity to obtain farm labour, particularly at this time of year when harvesting or seeding is taking place. The farmer actually loses money in other ways, too, because he has to over-mechanize his farming and buy bigger machines, bigger combines, bigger tractors so that he may finish his work with this bigger equipment, instead of employing farm labourers and using smaller equipment. If he were able to operate with smaller equipment, with the help of the farm labourer, he would save money.
I ask the minister to give serious consideration not only to bringing farm labourers under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act but to bringing the Gill report before this house for debate, so that representations can be made by members of parliament to the minister, and the government can live up to the recommendations contained in that report. Farmers are deprived of the opportunity to get men who are skilled in operating these machines, for the simple reason these men are not covered by unemployment insurance. I understand there is now a conference being held to see how we can train industrial workers so they may continue to be employed, in the face of automation. Why cannot farm labour be trained in the same way as industrial workers? Farming today is not what it used to be 25 years ago. Today it is mechanized and skilled labourers are required. Consequently seasonal labour is difficult to get.

I have referred the minister to this matter before and he is familiar with the subject. In 1956 some coverage was given to farm labour. For instance, it was extended to those concerned with the raising of poultry, egg grading, and the raising of racehorses, saddle horses and light harness horses. Then in 1957 the previous government included the self-employed fishermen. I do not say that the self-employed fishermen should not be covered because they do need assistance, but there were other methods to apply to the fishermen. This is why the farmers in the west, and I am sure also in the east, are so concerned that the self-employed fishermen are covered but farm labour is not covered. Not very long ago the national employment service held a number of meetings out of which recommendations were brought forward to train farm labour to operate some of the machines used today.
I would also direct the attention of the minister to the fact that on more than one occasion he has said that the Gill report will be brought in, but to date it has not been presented. If it is not presented during the remainder of this session-and I am sure we all agree it is too late now-then the minister should seriously consider bringing it down during the next session. The Gill report deserves more attention than it has received in the past.
Another matter with which I should like to deal is this. During the session many labour matters have been brought up, and I suggest that the training of industrial workers and farm labourers should also be considered. I am sure that as time goes on more and more skilled labour will be required on the farms. I have referred to this matter before and whenever I have the chance to go home this is one of the matters my constituents bring to my attention. They want an answer as to why farm labour is the only group which is being discriminated against. Whether or not the minister will deal with this matter when he answers some of the questions which have been put forward I do not know, but I am very serious about it. I should like the minister to explain, so that the farmers can understand why it is not possible for him to bring in the Gill report, and why it is not possible for him also to bring farm labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act. It has been suggested that contributions could be made on a voluntary basis, but the experts have explained that this would not work because the only ones who would pay into such a voluntary fund would be those who require permanent labour on farms, not seasonal.

Most labour on the farm is seasonal, particularly now that most of the farms are mechanized.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which I directed to the Minister of Defence Production earlier today related to the apparent plans of the government to conduct a public auction as a method of disposing of the buildings and facilities, and I suppose a certain amount of equipment,

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion at the former mid-Canada radar site at Bird, Manitoba, which has recently been phased out.
Since introducing this question earlier today the minister has informed me that a considerable amount of study has been given to the possibility of an alternate use for these facilities and that no satisfactory solution has been found. He has informed me that several government departments and agencies have been contacted as to any possible interest they might have in these facilities, but to date these inquiries have met with no success.
I realize that if this is the complete picture it is exceedingly difficult for a government to provide a satisfactory solution. However, it is my belief that this is what governments are for. This is one of their obligations, one of the responsibilities of their mandate.
It has always been my hope that possibly the Indian affairs branch would show a keen desire to take over these extremely modern facilities, move a number of Indian people of the north into these quarters under proper supervision and undertake any one of a number of possible industrial projects which would be of tremendous benefit to these unemployed people, who in many cases are living on welfare at the present time. They are also sorely in need of adequate housing, which is available at the present time at this site.
Many proposals have been presented to the government with regard to alternate uses for these facilities at this former mid-Canada site, including an elderly persons' hostel, particularly for elderly Indian people of northern Manitoba. This would make an ideal location for a project of that nature. It has also been suggested that the facilities could be used for a tuberculosis hospital for short term patients, or as a technical school for young people of Indian ancestry. This also could be carried out in conjunction with the Indian affairs branch. Time does not permit me to go over all the suggestions which have been advanced.
However, today I asked the minister to consider delaying the public auction until every possible alternate use by a government agency has been explored, and I hope the minister will see fit to do this. But if it is decided this cannot be done I would respectfully ask the minister to give the house every assurance that these facilities will not be disposed of to anyone who cannot assure the government or Crown Assets Disposal Corporation that their purpose in purchasing them will eventually provide employment for

a certain number of people, particularly the Indian people of northern Manitoba. I think every precaution should be taken to assure that the facilities are not disposed of to a private individual for a nominal sum for his own use.
I should also like to know how much advertising has been conducted in relation to the proposed auction, and how many people, and who, have been notified personally that such an auction is to take place.
Finally, I should like to run over briefly a few of the facilities which are at the site at Bird. The site is located on the Hudson Bay railway line at mile 347. There are good transportation facilities including a railway spur line into the site. There is a 2,400 foot gravel landing strip and a steel and concrete reinforced helicopter landing strip. Town streets and sidewalks are completed. The site is located on the banks of the Limestone river which flows into the Nelson river. It is in a well treed area and has a sandy and gravel soil with no permafrost.
The communications consist of a government licensed radio station, C.N.R. telegraph and a direct telephone connection with the Manitoba telephone system at The Pas.
There are two central steam heating plants to service all buildings with central heating, a fully modern sewage disposal plant capable of handling sewage disposal for a population of 5,000 people, storm sewers to handle excess surface water adequately at any time, a modern water treatment plant which services all buildings and is capable of handling a population of up to 5,000, a fully automatic dial telephone system connecting all buildings in the townsite and also connected to the Manitoba telephone system. In addition to this, there is power supplied by three Lister Blackstone generating units, supplying 250 kilowatts each and generating
4.000	volts. All buildings are equipped with a modern sprinkler system and fire alarm connected to a central fire hall. There is a tank farm located on the spur line offering six 5,000 gallon tanks and there are two
25.000	gallon tanks along with the No. 1 boiler house, and there are two 5,000 gallon tanks in the No. 1 boiler house-
